Fix an admissible multipointed Heegaard diagram with finitely many complementary regions. Fix generators $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$ and a vector $a\in\mathbb Z^k$. There are only finitely many nonnegative integral domains of Whitney disks from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$ whose $w$-multiplicity vector is $a$.

More generally, the same conclusion holds for any collection of nonnegative integral region chains whose pairwise differences are periodic domains and whose $w$-multiplicity vector is fixed. If an integer $s$ is prescribed instead of the vector, there are only finitely many such chains with $\sum_i n_{w_i}=s$. In particular this applies to a fixed-index collection whenever an independently established relative grading identity determines that sum from the endpoints and the index. This is finiteness of domains; it makes no assertion about the number of disk classes with a given domain or the compactness of a moduli space.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: Number the regions $R_1,\ldots,R_r$ and identify a region chain with its coefficient vector in $\mathbb R^r$. The condition that its boundary be a real linear combination of full attaching curves is a rational homogeneous linear condition: subdivide the curves at their finitely many intersections, write the cellular boundary of each region on the resulting oriented edges, and quotient the edge space by the span of the full curves, all of whose vectors are integral. Gaussian elimination over $\mathbb Q$ supplies a matrix with rational entries whose kernel is precisely this condition. Append the equations that the coefficients at the regions containing each $w_i$ vanish. Denote the resulting real kernel by $L$. Its integral vectors are exactly the integral periodic domains with zero $w$-multiplicities. Redundant edge subdivisions and equations do not affect this conclusion. [F1, construct, algebra]

We claim $L\cap\mathbb R_{\ge0}^r=\{0\}$. Otherwise take nonzero $v$ in this intersection and let $I=\{j:v_j>0\}$. In the rational linear subspace $L_I=L\cap\{v_j=0:j\notin I\}$, Gaussian elimination gives a basis of rational vectors. Express $v$ in that basis and approximate its finitely many real coefficients by rational numbers closely enough that all coordinates in $I$ remain positive. The resulting rational vector lies in $L_I$, is nonnegative and nonzero. Multiplying by a common positive denominator gives a nonzero nonnegative integral vector in $L$, contrary to admissibility. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

If the fixed-vector slice is empty there is nothing to prove. Otherwise fix a member $D_0$. Every other member $D$ lies in $(D_0+L)\cap\mathbb R_{\ge0}^r$: its difference from $D_0$ is periodic and has zero marked multiplicities. The integral members of this intersection are bounded. Otherwise enumerate $\mathbb Z^r$ once and for each positive integer $n$ take its first member $D_n$ in the intersection with $\|D_n\|>n$. This specifies the sequence without any choice principle. The nonnegative unit vectors $D_n/\|D_n\|$ have a convergent subsequence in the finite-dimensional unit sphere. Its limit $v$ is nonnegative with norm one; since $(D_n-D_0)/\|D_n\|\in L$ and a kernel of a matrix is closed, $v\in L$, contradicting step 2.1. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given]

A bounded subset of $\mathbb R^r$ has only finitely many integral vectors: a common bound on the coordinates places them in a finite product of finite integer intervals. This proves the fixed-vector assertion. Domains of two disks with the same endpoints have periodic difference: the endpoint corners cancel in their boundary difference, leaving on each attaching circle a cycle, whose integer edge coefficient is constant around that circle and hence an integer multiple of the full circle. Thus the assertion applies to the disk domains in the first paragraph. [step 3.1, algebra]

For nonnegative chains each $n_{w_i}$ is a nonnegative integer. If their sum is $s<0$ there are none; if $s\ge0$ each coordinate is one of $0,\ldots,s$, leaving finitely many vectors. Apply the fixed-vector result to each vector and take the finite union. If a relative grading identity fixes $\sum_i n_{w_i}$, this argument applies with that integer; it does not establish the identity itself or identify domains with homotopy classes. [step 4.1, algebra] ∎

Let $\Sigma$ be a closed Riemann surface, $m\ge1$, and $p\in\Sigma$. In the complex symmetric product $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ let $E_p=\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$. Let $L_0,L_1\subset X$ be compact submanifolds disjoint from $E_p$. Suppose $J_t$ agrees with the fixed complex structure of $X$ on one neighborhood of $E_p$ for every $t\in[0,1]$. Let $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to X$ be a smooth solution of $\partial_\tau u+J_t(u)\partial_tu=0$, with boundary on $L_0,L_1$ and uniform limits as $\tau\to\pm\infty$ at points of $L_0\cap L_1$.

The intersections of $u$ with $E_p$ are a finite collection of interior points, each with positive integral local intersection multiplicity. Their sum is nonnegative, and it is zero exactly when $u$ avoids $E_p$. In pointed Heegaard data, with $L_0,L_1$ the product tori and $p$ any marked point, this proves nonnegativity of the domain multiplicity $n_p(u)$ whenever it is defined by intersection with $E_p$.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: The divisor $E_p$ is a smooth complex hypersurface, including at tuples with repeated entries. To check this, choose pairwise disjoint coordinate disks about the distinct entries of a tuple, and use in each cluster the elementary symmetric functions of its local coordinates as coordinates on the corresponding symmetric power. This coordinate description follows directly by associating an unordered tuple to the coefficients of its monic polynomial; conversely its roots, counted with multiplicity, recover the tuple. In the cluster containing $p$, choose its coordinate to put $p$ at zero. The condition that a root be zero is the vanishing of the constant coefficient, which is one of these complex coordinates. Thus near every point of $E_p$ there is a holomorphic coordinate function $h$ with nonvanishing differential such that $E_p=\{h=0\}$. [given, construct, algebra]

On a small interior disk mapped into such a neighborhood, $f=h\circ u$ is scalar holomorphic. In fact the equation there is $u_t=J_0u_\tau$; holomorphicity of $h$ gives $f_t=i f_\tau$, the ordinary Cauchy–Riemann equation for the coordinate $\tau+it$. The set of interior points having a neighborhood mapped entirely into $E_p$ is open and closed in the connected strip interior. For closedness, at a limit point use one defining coordinate $h$ on a small disk. If the limit point is not already in that set, [F1] makes its zero isolated, contradicting the presence of nearby open zero neighborhoods. The entire interior cannot map into $E_p$, since continuity would put the boundary in the closed set $E_p$, whereas $L_0,L_1$ avoid it. Thus the set is empty, and [F1] makes every intersection isolated with a positive finite zero order. [step 1.1, F1, given]

All intersections lie in a compact subset of the strip interior. Uniform convergence at both ends, and the fact that both limit points avoid the closed divisor, exclude sufficiently long ends. On the remaining compact rectangle, its two boundary edges have compact image disjoint from $E_p$, so continuity excludes a neighborhood of those edges. The remaining preimage of $E_p$ is closed in a compact interior rectangle. An infinite subset would have an accumulation point there, contradicting isolation in step 2.1. Hence there are finitely many intersections. [step 2.1, given]

At one such intersection, write $h\circ u=(z-a)^r g(z)$ as in [F1], with $g$ nonzero on a small closed disk. The local intersection number is the winding number of $h\circ u$ on its positively oriented boundary in the oriented complex normal line to $E_p$. This is $r$: the factor $(z-a)^r$ winds $r$ times, while $g$ has winding zero because its nonvanishing extension over the disk contracts its boundary loop. Replacing $h$ by another holomorphic defining function multiplies it by a nowhere-zero holomorphic function, which has winding zero by the same argument. Thus the intersection multiplicity is intrinsic and positive. The finite sum is zero exactly when the intersection set is empty. The marked-point domain coefficient defined by this intersection number is that sum. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, algebra] ∎

existing_donor_fragment.statement_excerpt:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M,N$ be Hausdorff second-countable $C^r$ manifolds modeled on separable real Hilbert spaces, and let $f:M\to N$ be $C^r$, where $r$ is a positive integer or $\infty$. Suppose every derivative $Df(x)$ is a bounded Fredholm operator of the same index $d$ and $r>\max\{d,0\}$. Then the regular values of $f$ form a dense residual subset of $N$. A value is regular if every derivative at its inverse images is surjective; values with empty inverse image are regular.

Here Hilbert completeness means convergence of Cauchy sequences. No arbitrary-index choice or dependent-choice axiom is assumed. This theorem concerns a map already known to be Fredholm; it does not establish Fredholmness of a differential operator or transversality of its universal solution space.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: We first establish the needed complete-space facts with the indicated choice strength. Every subspace $S$ of a separable metric space is separable under countable choice: enumerate its ambient rational-radius balls with centers in a fixed countable dense set, and for each ball meeting $S$ select a point of its intersection with $S$ by [F2]. Those selected points are dense in $S$. Complete separable metric spaces satisfy the Baire conclusion by a deterministic construction. Given closed nowhere dense sets $A_n$ and a nonempty open set $O$, enumerate the same kind of balls; recursively take the first ball whose closed ball lies in the preceding open ball minus $A_n$, has positive radius at most $2^{-n}$, and, at the first stage, has closed ball in $O$. Such a ball exists because $A_n$ has empty interior. The centers form a Cauchy sequence; its limit belongs to every closed ball and hence to $O\setminus\bigcup_n A_n$. This uses recursion with a uniquely specified next ball, not dependent choice. It applies equally inside any open subset by keeping the first closed ball inside that subset. [F2, given, construct]

For a closed linear subspace $S$ of a separable real Hilbert space $H$, fix $x\in H$ and put $a=\inf_{s\in S}\|x-s\|$. Use a countable dense sequence in $S$ from step 1.1 and take its first point $s_n$ satisfying $\|x-s_n\|^2<a^2+1/n$. The parallelogram identity gives $$\|s_n-s_j\|^2=2\|x-s_n\|^2+2\|x-s_j\|^2-4\left\|x-\frac{s_n+s_j}{2}\right\|^2\le 2/n+2/j.$$ The limit $s\in S$ minimizes the distance. The inequality $\|x-s-tv\|^2\ge\|x-s\|^2$ for all real $t$ and $v\in S$ forces $\langle x-s,v\rangle=0$. Thus $H=S\oplus S^\perp$, uniquely; the projection onto $S$ is linear and has norm at most one, by Pythagoras. This proves the splitting without Hahn–Banach. [step 1.1, algebra, construct]

A bounded surjection $T:E\to F$ between separable Banach spaces is open under the same hypothesis. Indeed $F=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\overline{T(B_E(0,n))}$. By step 1.1 some member has interior. Subtracting two points of a small ball in this interior shows that for some $c>0$, $$B_F(0,c)\subseteq\overline{T(B_E(0,1))}.$$ Here subtraction of limits of images of two radius-$n$ balls gives a radius-$2n$ ball before rescaling. For $\|y\|<c/2$ choose successively $x_j$ with $\|x_j\|<2^{-j}$ and residual $\|y-T\sum_{i=1}^j x_i\|<c2^{-j-1}$, starting at $j=1$. At each step the displayed closure inclusion rescaled by $2^{-j}$ permits this approximation; take the first qualifying element of a fixed dense sequence in the open ball of radius $2^{-j}$, since the inequalities are open. The sum converges in $E$, has norm less than one, and maps to $y$. Thus $B_F(0,c/2)\subseteq T(B_E(0,1))$. Rescaling and translating proves openness. In particular a bounded bijection has bounded inverse. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

We also need the local inverse theorem with no stronger choice. If a $C^r$ map $g$ between open subsets of real Hilbert spaces has boundedly invertible derivative $A$ at zero, translate so $g(0)=0$ and choose $R>0$ with the closed radius-$R$ ball in its domain and $\|I-A^{-1}Dg(x)\|\le1/2$ on that ball. The mean-value estimate along a segment gives that $T_y(x)=x-A^{-1}(g(x)-y)$ is a contraction of ratio $1/2$ and maps the ball into itself when $\|A^{-1}y\|<R/2$. The estimate follows without any vector integration theorem: apply each continuous real linear functional of norm one to the segment curve and the scalar mean-value inequality, then take the supremum; for Hilbert targets the required norming functional is explicitly the inner product with the normalized difference. The deterministic iterates $x_{n+1}=T_y(x_n)$, $x_0=0$, have a geometric Cauchy bound and converge to the unique fixed point. Thus $g$ has an inverse on a neighborhood of zero. Comparison of fixed-point equations makes this inverse locally Lipschitz. [step 2.2, construct, algebra]

This inverse is $C^r$. The operators $Dg(x)$ near zero have bounded inverses by the norm-convergent series for $(I-(I-A^{-1}Dg(x)))^{-1}A^{-1}$. If $g^{-1}(y+h)=x+k$, the Lipschitz estimate gives $\|k\|=O(\|h\|)$ and differentiability gives $h=Dg(x)k+o(\|k\|)$, so $Dg^{-1}(y)=Dg(x)^{-1}$. Inversion of boundedly invertible operators is smooth: writing $(B+H)^{-1}=(I+B^{-1}H)^{-1}B^{-1}$ and using the convergent geometric series shows the first derivative $H\mapsto-B^{-1}HB^{-1}$, with a remainder bounded by a constant times $\|H\|^2$ locally; repeated differentiation of this product gives derivatives of every order, finite sums of products of inverses and increments. The chain and product rules and induction now give the claimed $C^r$ regularity of $g^{-1}$, also for $r=\infty$. All limits in this argument are of specified sequences. [step 3.1, algebra]

Work in charts about $x\in M$ and $f(x)\in N$, translate both coordinate origins, and write $L=Df(0)$. By step 2.1 split the domain as $K\oplus E_1$, with $K=\ker L$, and the target as $R\oplus Q$, with $R=\operatorname{ran}L$. The spaces $K,Q$ are finite dimensional by Fredholmness, $R$ is closed, and $E_1=K^\perp$. The restriction $L:E_1\to R$ is a bounded bijection and has bounded inverse by step 2.2. Write $f=(\rho,c)$ in the target splitting. The map $$ (v,z)\longmapsto(\rho(v+z),v)\quad (v\in K,\ z\in E_1) $$ has boundedly invertible derivative $(v,z)\mapsto(Lz,v)$ at zero. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 give a local $C^r$ inverse. Shrink its image to a product $U\times A$, with $U\subset R$, $A\subset K$ open. In these coordinates $f$ has the form $(u,v)\mapsto(u,h(u,v))$, where $h:U\times A\to Q$ is $C^r$ and $\dim K-\dim Q=d$. The coordinate changes need only be compatible local coordinate changes; they need not be members of the originally specified atlas. [F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

In each such normal-form neighborhood choose a product of closed positive-radius balls $C=\overline B_R\times\overline B_K$ whose product lies in $U\times A$, and let $C$ also denote its inverse image in $M$. Its interior contains its center, it is closed relative to that normal-form neighborhood, and $f|_C$ is proper into the target chart. To verify properness, the first coordinates of inverse images of a compact target set lie in a compact subset of $R$, while their second coordinates lie in the compact finite-dimensional ball $\overline B_K$. The inverse-image set is closed in that compact product by continuity and the closed-ball conditions, hence compact. No compactness of an infinite-dimensional ball is asserted. [step 5.1, construct]

The interiors of all these blocks cover $M$. Choose a countable base $(B_i)$ of $M$. For each nonempty $B_i$ contained in the interior of some block, [F2] selects one witnessing block together with its normal-form neighborhood and target chart. There are countably many such indices, and their chosen interiors still cover $M$: for every point, first use any covering block and then a base member containing the point and contained in its interior. Relabel the chosen blocks $C_i$, neighborhoods $W_i$, and target charts $V_i$. This is one explicit countable-choice use, with the family fixed in advance; no selections indexed by all points of $M$ were made. [F2, step 6.1, construct]

Let $A_i=C_i\cap\operatorname{Crit}(f)$. In the normal form of step 5.1, surjectivity of $Df$ is equivalent to surjectivity of the finite-dimensional matrix $D_vh$. Thus the critical set is closed in $W_i$, because nonsurjectivity of such matrices is closed; hence $A_i$ is closed in $C_i$. Its image $D_i=f(A_i)$ is closed relative to $V_i$. For a direct verification, if $y_n\in D_i$ tends to $y\in V_i$, countable choice selects $x_n\in A_i$ over $y_n$. Properness places these points in the compact inverse image of $\{y\}\cup\{y_n:n\ge1\}$. In normal-form coordinates compactness gives a convergent subsequence with limit in $A_i$, mapping to $y$. This proves sequential closedness, which is closedness in the metrizable chart. [F2, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1]

The set $D_i$ has empty interior in $V_i$. If $Q=\{0\}$ in this block, all derivatives are onto and $D_i$ is empty. Otherwise a nonempty product open set $U'\times Q'$ in $D_i$ would, for any fixed $u\in U'$, make every point of $Q'$ a critical value of the finite-dimensional $C^r$ map $v\mapsto h(u,v)$ on its open kernel-coordinate domain. The inequality $r>\max\{\dim K-\dim Q,0\}$ is exactly the hypothesis of [F1]. For $r=\infty$ apply [F1] at any finite differentiability order above that bound. This contradicts [F1]. Thus $D_i$ is closed and nowhere dense relative to $V_i$. It is nowhere dense in $N$ as well: its closure in $N$ lies in $\overline V_i$, and any nonempty open subset of that closure must meet $V_i$, since the boundary of an open set has empty interior. Such an intersection would contradict its relative nowhere density. [F1, step 5.1, step 8.1, cases]

Every critical point lies in some $C_i$, so the nonregular values are exactly $\bigcup_i D_i$. Step 9.1 makes this a meagre subset of $N$, proving residuality of its complement. To see density, take any nonempty open subset of $N$, pass to a chart and then a nonempty open coordinate ball with closed ball still in the chart. The closures of the $D_i$ restrict there to closed nowhere dense sets. The deterministic Baire construction of step 1.1 gives a point in this ball outside them all. It is a regular value. The empty-manifold cases are immediate, and values outside $f(M)$ are included because their fibres have no nonsurjective derivative. [F2, step 1.1, step 7.1, step 9.1] ∎

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $m\ge1$ and angles $0<\theta_j<\pi$ for $1\le j\le m$. On the strip $S=\mathbb R\times[0,1]$ impose the real product-plane boundary conditions $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$ and $u(s,1)\in\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$. Let $H^1_\theta$ be the completion of smooth maps satisfying these conditions and compactly supported in the $s$ direction, for the norm
$$\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|u_s\|_2^2+\|u_t\|_2^2.$$
The real linear operator $D=\partial_s+i\partial_t$ extends to an isomorphism $H^1_\theta\to L^2(S;\mathbb C^m)$. Put $\gamma=\min_j\{\theta_j,\pi-\theta_j\}>0$. Its inverse satisfies
$$\|D^{-1}f\|_2\le\gamma^{-1}\|f\|_2,\qquad \|D^{-1}f\|_{H^1}\le\sqrt{\gamma^{-2}+5}\,\|f\|_2.$$
For $0\le\delta<\gamma$, set $w(s)=e^{\delta|s|}$, $H^1_{\theta,\delta}=\{u:wu\in H^1_\theta\}$ with norm $\|wu\|_{H^1}$, and $L^2_\delta=\{f:wf\in L^2\}$ with norm $\|wf\|_2$. Then $D:H^1_{\theta,\delta}\to L^2_\delta$ is an isomorphism and
$$\|D^{-1}f\|_{H^1_{\theta,\delta}}\le\frac{\sqrt{\gamma^{-2}+5}}{1-\delta/\gamma}\,\|f\|_{L^2_\delta},\qquad \|wD^{-1}f\|_2\le\frac{\|wf\|_2}{\gamma-\delta}.$$
These are estimates for the constant linear asymptotic model. They make no assertion about nonlinear strip decay, a variable-coefficient operator, or its Maslov index.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: For one component set $\lambda_n=\pi n-\theta$ and $e_n(t)=e^{-i\lambda_nt}$ for $n\in\mathbb Z$. These satisfy the specified real boundary lines, $i e'_n=\lambda_ne_n$, and form an orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1];\mathbb C)$ with pairing $\operatorname{Re}\int v\overline z$. Orthogonality follows by integrating $\cos(\pi(n-l)t)$. For completeness, multiply $v(t)$ by $e^{-i\theta t}$, reflect to $[-1,0]$ by $g(-t)=\overline{g(t)}$, and regard the extension as a length-two periodic $L^2$ function. Its complex Fourier coefficient at mode $e^{-i\pi nt}$ is real and equals $\operatorname{Re}\int_0^1g(t)e^{i\pi nt}\,dt$, precisely the real coefficient of $v$ at $e_n$. Fourier completeness in [F1] proves real completeness, and the Parseval identity follows by the same extension, whose squared norm is twice that of $g$ on $[0,1]$. Moreover $|\lambda_n|\ge\min\{\theta,\pi-\theta\}$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

For a real $b\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ and $\lambda\ne0$, define $$a(s)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{s}e^{-\lambda(s-r)}b(r)\,dr,&\lambda>0,\\\displaystyle-\int_s^{\infty}e^{-\lambda(s-r)}b(r)\,dr,&\lambda<0.\end{cases}$$ The absolute value of the kernel is nonnegative with $L^1$ norm $|\lambda|^{-1}$. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|a(s)|^2\le |\lambda|^{-1}\int |K(s-r)|\,|b(r)|^2dr$; integration and [F3] give $\|a\|_2\le|\lambda|^{-1}\|b\|_2$. Initially for smooth compactly supported $b$, direct differentiation proves $a'+\lambda a=b$, hence $\|a'\|_2\le2\|b\|_2$ and $\|\lambda a\|_2\le\|b\|_2$. Approximation by [F2] passes these identities to every $b\in L^2$, with the derivative in the weak sense. There is no other $H^1$ solution: a difference has $(e^{\lambda s}a)'=0$ distributionally and hence equals $Ce^{-\lambda s}$, which is in $L^2(\mathbb R)$ only if $C=0$. To justify the distributional constant assertion, any smooth compact test of integral zero is the derivative of another compactly supported smooth test; a distribution annihilating all such tests is a constant distribution. [F2, F3, construct, algebra]

For a smooth compactly supported boundary-compatible map write $a_{j,n}(s)=\operatorname{Re}\int_0^1 u_j(s,t)\overline{e_{j,n}(t)}\,dt$. Differentiation in $s$ commutes with this integral. Integration by parts in $t$ shows that the coefficient of $i u_t$ is $\lambda_{j,n}a_{j,n}$: the real part of its boundary term $iu_j\overline{e_{j,n}}$ vanishes at both ends because the factors there are on the same real line. Parseval and [F3] give $$\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\sum_{j,n}\int_{\mathbb R}\left(|a'_{j,n}|^2+(1+\lambda_{j,n}^2)|a_{j,n}|^2\right)ds.$$ Thus finite modal truncations converge in $H^1$, and $D$ acts on coefficients as $a\mapsto a'+\lambda a$. Each truncation is still smooth, compactly supported in $s$, and satisfies the boundary conditions. Passing to the completion preserves these identities and identifies its elements with coefficient families of finite displayed norm. Conversely every such family is obtained by first truncating its countable mode sum and then using [F2] for its finitely many $H^1(\mathbb R)$ coefficients. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

Apply step 1.2 to each real coefficient of $f$, using the modes of step 1.1 componentwise. By step 2.1 the resulting family is an element $u\in H^1_\theta$ and $Du=f$, with $$\|u\|_2^2\le\gamma^{-2}\|f\|_2^2,\qquad \|u_s\|_2^2\le4\|f\|_2^2,\qquad \|u_t\|_2^2\le\|f\|_2^2.$$ For a finite smooth modal forcing the convolution solutions are smooth with exponential tails, so multiplying by cutoffs tending to one also places them in the defining completion; this is consistent with the coefficient characterization in step 2.1. The scalar uniqueness assertion proves injectivity. The estimate $\|Du\|_2\le\|u_s\|_2+\|u_t\|_2$ proves boundedness of $D$, while the displayed bounds prove boundedness of its inverse $Q$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]

Multiplication by the locally Lipschitz scalar $w=e^{\delta|s|}$ preserves the real boundary conditions and obeys the weak product rule locally. Explicitly $w'=\delta\operatorname{sign}(s)w$ almost everywhere, with no point-mass term at zero because $w$ is continuous. The rule follows first by integrating by parts separately on the two half-strips, whose boundary terms at zero cancel, and then by local $H^1$ approximation, supplied by the finite modal truncations and [F2] in step 2.1. Hence conjugating the weighted problem by $v=wu$ gives $$wD(w^{-1}v)=Dv-Bv,\qquad Bv=\delta\operatorname{sign}(s)v.$$ This also shows that $D$ maps the stated weighted domain boundedly to $L^2_\delta$. [F2, step 2.1, given, algebra]

On $L^2$ the operator $BQ$ has norm at most $\delta/\gamma<1$, by step 3.1. Thus $(I-BQ)^{-1}=\sum_{r\ge0}(BQ)^r$ converges in operator norm, and $$v=Q(I-BQ)^{-1}(wf)$$ is the unique solution of $(D-B)v=wf$. Indeed $(D-B)Q=I-BQ$, and for any $v\in H^1_\theta$, $QDv=v$ gives $v=Q(D-B)v+QBv$; the norm bound $\|QB\|_{L^2\to L^2}<1$ proves the homogeneous solution is zero. The norm of the inverse series is at most $(1-\delta/\gamma)^{-1}$. Combining this with the $H^1$ and $L^2$ bounds for $Q$ in step 3.1 proves both weighted inequalities, and step 3.2 carries existence and uniqueness back to $u=w^{-1}v$. [step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

Assume Countable Choice. On $S=\mathbb R\times[0,1]$ use the real Hilbert domain $H^1_\theta$ with product-line boundary conditions at angles $0<\theta_j<\pi$: it is the $H^1$ completion of smooth maps compactly supported in the first coordinate and satisfying $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$, $u(s,1)\in\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$. Let $B(s,t)$ be a bounded measurable real linear endomorphism of $\mathbb C^m$. Suppose there are real diagonal constant matrices $B_\pm=\operatorname{diag}(b_{\pm,1},\ldots,b_{\pm,m})$ such that
$$\underset{\pm s>R,\ 0<t<1}{\operatorname{ess\,sup}}\|B(s,t)-B_\pm\|\longrightarrow0\quad(R\longrightarrow\infty),$$
and $\theta_j-b_{\pm,j}\notin\pi\mathbb Z$ for every $j$ and each sign. Then
$$T=\partial_s+i\partial_t+B(s,t):H^1_\theta\longrightarrow L^2(S;\mathbb C^m)$$
is bounded and Fredholm over $\mathbb R$: its kernel and cokernel are finite dimensional and its range is closed. There are bounded left and right parametrices whose errors are operator-norm limits of finite-rank operators. No index value or identification with a Maslov index is asserted.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: Set $X=H^1_\theta$ and $Y=L^2(S;\mathbb C^m)$ with their real Hilbert structures. The operator $T:X\to Y$ is bounded because $B$ is essentially bounded and both first derivatives are controlled by the $X$ norm. There are bounded inverses $Q_0$ for $D$ and $Q_\pm$ for $D+B_\pm$. For the latter take $\phi_{\pm,j}\in(0,\pi)$ representing $\theta_j-b_{\pm,j}$ modulo $\pi$. The multiplication $U_\pm(t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{ib_{\pm,j}t})$ maps $H^1_{\phi_\pm}$ boundedly and invertibly onto $X$, since its derivative is bounded and it maps the endpoint real lines to the desired lines. Direct differentiation gives $(D+B_\pm)U_\pm v=U_\pm Dv$. Thus [F1] provides $Q_\pm=U_\pm D_{\phi_\pm}^{-1}U_\pm^{-1}$. These identities hold on the dense smooth subspaces and hence on their completions. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

Restriction $X\to L^2([-R,R]\times[0,1])$ is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank maps for each positive integer $R$. Indeed partition the rectangle into squares of side $h=1/N$ and replace a function on each square $C$ by its average $u_C$. For smooth $u$, the variance identity and the coordinate-segment fundamental theorem of calculus give $$\int_C|u-u_C|^2=\frac1{2|C|}\int_C\int_C|u(x)-u(y)|^2dxdy\le h^2\int_C(|u_s|^2+|u_t|^2).$$ For the inequality insert the intermediate point $(y_1,x_2)$, bound the square of the sum by twice the sum of squares, and bound each coordinate difference by $h$ times the integral of the squared corresponding derivative along that segment; integrating the other coordinates and dividing by $2h^2$ gives the displayed bound. Sum over the finite grid and pass to the defining smooth completion of $X$. The cell-average map has finite-dimensional range and its error has norm at most $h$. Consequently multiplication $X\to Y$ by any bounded measurable matrix or scalar supported in such a rectangle is a norm limit of finite-rank maps: compose restriction, cell averaging, and multiplication. No extension theorem or general Rellich theorem is used. [F1, construct, algebra]

We record the elementary Hilbert facts used below under precisely Countable Choice. Every closed subspace $Z$ of a Hilbert space has an orthogonal projection: for $x$, countable choice selects $z_n\in Z$ with $\|x-z_n\|^2<a^2+1/n$, where $a=\inf_{z\in Z}\|x-z\|$. The parallelogram identity makes $(z_n)$ Cauchy, because $\|z_n-z_l\|^2\le2/n+2/l$. Its limit $z\in Z$ minimizes the distance; applying minimality to $z+tv$ for all real $t$ gives $x-z\perp Z$. Uniqueness then makes the projection linear and contractive. In particular a closed subspace and its orthogonal complement give an orthogonal direct sum. Also the image of the unit ball under a norm limit of finite-rank operators is totally bounded: approximate the operator within any given positive tolerance and use a finite net for the bounded finite-dimensional image. Every sequence in such an image has a Cauchy subsequence, by taking at each successively finer finite cover the first member containing infinitely many of the remaining indices and then taking the least next index; completeness gives convergence. Countable choice suffices to select finite covers at the countably many scales in advance, and the subsequent recursion is deterministic. [given, construct, algebra]

Here is the needed parametrix criterion, proved without a general Atkinson theorem. Suppose a bounded operator $A:H\to G$ between real Hilbert spaces has bounded $L:G\to H$, $R:G\to H$ with $LA=I+K_H$ and $AR=I+K_G$, where both $K$'s are norm limits of finite-rank maps. Then $\ker A$ is finite dimensional. Choose a finite-rank $F$ with $\|K_H-F\|<1/2$. For $x\in\ker A$, $x=-K_Hx$ implies $\|x\|\le\|Fx\|+\|x\|/2$. Thus $F$ is injective on the kernel, identifying it with a subspace of its finite-dimensional range. [step 1.3, construct, algebra]

Construct parametrices for $T$ as follows. Choose three smooth scalar cutoffs $\chi_-,\chi_0,\chi_+$ with $\chi_-^2+\chi_0^2+\chi_+^2=1$, the first supported in $s<-R$, the last in $s>R$, and $\chi_0$ compactly supported. They can have first derivatives bounded by a constant independent of $R$: take fixed smooth transitions over intervals of width one at the two ends and use sine and cosine of a transition angle to obtain a squared partition. Their multiplication norms on both $X$ and $Y$ are then uniformly bounded. Write $B_0=0$, and set $$S=\chi_-Q_-\chi_-+\chi_0Q_0\chi_0+\chi_+Q_+\chi_+:Y\to X.$$ The product rule and $(D+B_i)Q_i=I$, $Q_i(D+B_i)=I$ give $$TS=I+\sum_i\bigl(\chi_i(B-B_i)Q_i\chi_i+\chi_i'Q_i\chi_i\bigr),\qquad ST=I+\sum_i\bigl(\chi_iQ_i\chi_i(B-B_i)-\chi_iQ_i\chi_i'\bigr).$$ These hold first for the defining smooth subspace and then by boundedness. Bounded measurable $B$ requires no derivative in these identities. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

The range of $A$ is closed. Put $Z=(\ker A)^\perp$. There is $c>0$ with $\|Ax\|\ge c\|x\|$ for $x\in Z$. Otherwise Countable Choice chooses unit vectors $x_n\in Z$ with $\|Ax_n\|<1/n$. Step 1.3 supplies a subsequence on which $K_Hx_n$ converges. The identity $x_n=LAx_n-K_Hx_n$ then makes $x_n$ converge in $H$ to a unit vector in $Z\cap\ker A$, impossible. Given a convergent sequence $Ax_n$ in the range, replace each $x_n$ by its orthogonal projection onto $Z$; the lower bound makes these new preimages Cauchy, and their limit maps to the specified target limit. Thus the range is sequentially closed and hence closed in the metric space $G$. [step 1.3, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

In the two formulas of step 2.2, the $i=0$ term involving $B$ and all the terms with $\chi_i'$ are norm limits of finite-rank maps by step 1.2 and bounded composition. For example $\chi_0BQ_0\chi_0:Y\to Y$ uses the compactly supported multiplier $\chi_0B:X\to Y$ after $Q_0\chi_0$, while $\chi_0Q_0\chi_0 B:X\to X$ uses that multiplier before $\chi_0Q_0$. The analogous derivative terms use $\chi_i':X\to Y$. In the remaining exterior terms $\|B-B_\pm\|$ is uniformly as small as desired when $R$ is large. Since $Q_i$ are fixed and the cutoff multiplication norms are uniformly bounded, the sum of those exterior terms has operator norm below $1/2$ on $Y$ in the first identity and on $X$ in the second, for one sufficiently large $R$. Thus $$TS=I+E_Y+K_Y,\qquad ST=I+E_X+K_X,$$ where $\|E_Y\|,\|E_X\|<1/2$ and both $K$'s are norm limits of finite-rank maps. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, given, algebra]

Its cokernel is finite dimensional as well. Let $P$ be the orthogonal projection onto $(\operatorname{ran}A)^\perp$, which exists by step 3.1 and step 1.3. From $AR=I+K_G$ one gets $y=-PK_Gy$ for $y\in(\operatorname{ran}A)^\perp$. Approximate $K_G$ within $1/2$ by finite-rank $F$. Then $\|y\|\le\|PFy\|+\|y\|/2$, so $PF$ is injective on this orthogonal complement. It is therefore finite dimensional. The orthogonal decomposition identifies $G/\operatorname{ran}A$ linearly with that complement. This completes the criterion. [step 1.3, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

The geometric series give bounded inverses of $I+E_X$ and $I+E_Y$. Set $L=(I+E_X)^{-1}S$ and $R_0=S(I+E_Y)^{-1}$. Then $$LT=I+(I+E_X)^{-1}K_X,\qquad TR_0=I+K_Y(I+E_Y)^{-1}.$$ The remainders are still norm limits of finite-rank maps, since composition by a bounded operator preserves that property. Apply the criterion of steps 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1 with $A=T$. This proves finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel, closed range, and the promised parametrices, with Countable Choice as the only choice axiom used. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

Assume Countable Choice. Let $v:[0,\infty)\times[0,1]\to\mathbb C^m$ be smooth, with $v(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$, $v(s,1)\in\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$, where $0<\theta_j<\pi$. Suppose its Dirichlet energy $\int(|v_s|^2+|v_t|^2)$ is finite and it satisfies almost everywhere
$$v_s+iv_t=A(s,t)v_s+C(s,t)v_t+E(s,t)v,$$
where $A,C,E$ are bounded measurable real linear endomorphisms. Put $\gamma=\min_j\{\theta_j,\pi-\theta_j\}$, fix $0<\delta<\gamma$, and set
$$M_\delta=\frac{\sqrt{\gamma^{-2}+5}}{1-\delta/\gamma}.$$
If $\|A\|_\infty+\|C\|_\infty+\|E\|_\infty\le\varepsilon$ and $M_\delta(1+\delta)\varepsilon\le1/2$, then for every smooth scalar cutoff $\chi$ equal to zero near $s=0$ and to one for $s\ge1$, with $0\le\chi\le1$, the zero extension to the full strip of $e^{\delta s}\chi v$ belongs to $H^1_\theta$ and
$$\|e^{\delta s}\chi v\|_{H^1}\le2M_\delta e^\delta(1+\varepsilon)\|\chi'v\|_2.$$
In particular $v$ and its first derivatives are exponentially square-integrable on $s\ge1$, and $\|v(s,\cdot)\|_{L^2([0,1])}=O(e^{-\delta s})$ there. The assertion also applies when the coefficients depend on $v$ and its derivatives, provided the displayed measurable-coefficient bound holds along the given solution. It is an analytic estimate with exact linear boundary conditions; no geometric flattening or higher-derivative regularity assertion is included.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: At each fixed $s$, expand $v(s,\cdot)$ in the modes from [F1]. The integration-by-parts and Parseval calculation there gives $\|v(s,\cdot)\|_2\le\gamma^{-1}\|v_t(s,\cdot)\|_2$, because every eigenvalue has absolute value at least $\gamma$. Integrating in $s$ shows $v\in L^2$ on the half-strip. Together with finite Dirichlet energy this makes $u=\chi v$, extended by zero before $s=0$, an element of $H^1_\theta$: it vanishes near the joining edge, and cutoffs tending to one in the $s$ direction approximate it in $H^1$ by the defining smooth boundary-compatible maps. Extend $A,C,E$ by zero to $s<0$. The product rule gives $$Du=Au_s+Cu_t+Eu+f,\qquad f=(I-A)\chi'v.$$ The forcing is supported in $0\le s\le1$ and $\|f\|_2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|\chi'v\|_2$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

For any bounded measurable scalar $q(s)$ with $\|q\|_\infty\le\delta$, the operator $D-q$ has inverse $Q(I-qQ)^{-1}:L^2\to H^1_\theta$ of norm at most $M_\delta$. Indeed $\|qQ\|_{L^2\to L^2}\le\delta/\gamma<1$, so its geometric series converges and $(D-q)Q=I-qQ$. Conversely $h\in\ker(D-q)$ satisfies $h=Qqh$, and the same strict $L^2$ contraction forces $h=0$. Thus this is a two-sided inverse. This argument permits discontinuous $q$ and does not differentiate it. [F1, algebra]

For each positive integer $N$ set $w_N(s)=\exp(\delta\min\{\max\{s,0\},N\})$ and $q_N=w_N'/w_N$, defined almost everywhere. Then $w_N$ is bounded and locally Lipschitz with $0\le q_N\le\delta$, and $z_N=w_Nu\in H^1_\theta$. The product rule, justified on each interval and across the continuous joins as in [F1], turns step 1.1 into $$(D-q_N)z_N=A(z_N)_s+C(z_N)_t+(E-Aq_N)z_N+w_Nf.$$ The norm of the first three terms on the right is at most $(1+\delta)\varepsilon\|z_N\|_{H^1}$. Apply step 1.2 and the assumed smallness to absorb that term, giving $$\|z_N\|_{H^1}\le2M_\delta\|w_Nf\|_2\le2M_\delta e^\delta\|f\|_2.$$ This bound is uniform in $N$; the capped weights make each application legitimate before any exponential integrability is known. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, construct, algebra]

On every fixed bounded interval of positive $s$, for all sufficiently large $N$ one has $z_N=e^{\delta s}u$ and the same equality for its weak first derivatives. The uniform bound in step 2.1 therefore bounds the integrals of the squared function and derivatives on every bounded rectangle by its squared right-hand side. Exhausting the strip by these rectangles proves $z=e^{\delta s}u\in H^1$ with that bound. Its boundary conditions persist, and $s$ cutoffs approximate it in the defining $H^1_\theta$ norm; local smoothness of $u$ and the mode characterization in [F1] give membership in that completion. Step 1.1 now proves the displayed estimate. On $s\ge1$ we have $z=e^{\delta s}v$, $e^{\delta s}v_t=z_t$, and $e^{\delta s}v_s=z_s-\delta z$, proving exponential square-integrability of all three quantities. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

Finally regard $z(s,\cdot)$ for $s\ge1$ as a curve with values in $L^2([0,1];\mathbb C^m)$. Its squared norm has derivative $2\operatorname{Re}\langle z_s,z\rangle$, first for finite modal sums and then by their $H^1$ convergence from [F1]. There is a sequence $s_n\to\infty$ with $\|z(s_n,\cdot)\|_2\to0$, since $z$ is square-integrable in $s$. Integrating the derivative from $s$ to $s_n$, then using Cauchy–Schwarz and passing to infinity gives $$\|z(s,\cdot)\|_2^2\le2\int_s^\infty\|z_s(r,\cdot)\|_2\|z(r,\cdot)\|_2dr\le\|z\|_{H^1([1,\infty)\times[0,1])}^2.$$ This holds for the continuous $L^2$ representative, which agrees with the given smooth $v$. Multiplying by $e^{-2\delta s}$ proves the claimed exponential $L^2$ slice bound. Dependence of the coefficients on the solution changes none of the preceding estimates, which use only their values and stated bounds along that solution. [F1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(\Sigma,j)$ be a closed Riemann surface with positive area form $\eta$, and put $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$, $m\ge1$, with its induced complex structure $J_0$. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to X$ be the quotient, $\Delta\subset X$ its repeated-point locus, and $\Omega=\sum_{l=1}^m\operatorname{pr}_l^*\eta$. Off $\Delta$ the permutation-invariant form $\Omega$ descends to a smooth form $\omega$ on $X\setminus\Delta$. Equip $X$ with any smooth Riemannian metric $g$.

Let $L_\alpha,L_\beta$ be product tori formed from two finite systems of pairwise disjoint attaching curves, with transverse intersections between the systems. Suppose a smooth path $J_t$ agrees with $J_0$ on a neighborhood $V$ of $\Delta$ and tames $\omega$ on $X\setminus V$. Let $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to X$ be a smooth $J_t$-holomorphic strip, with boundary on these tori, finite $g$-Dirichlet energy, and uniform limits at both ends to intersection generators. For each complementary region $R$ of the attaching curves write $n_R(u)$ for the signed intersection multiplicity of $u$ with $\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$ at a generic $p\in R$.

There is a constant $C$ depending only on the fixed geometric data and the path, independent of $u$, such that
$$E_g(u)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R\times[0,1]}(|u_s|_g^2+|u_t|_g^2)\,dsdt\le C\sum_R n_R(u)\int_R\eta.$$
In particular energies of all such representatives with one fixed domain are uniformly bounded. The finite-energy hypothesis here is explicit; no assertion that arbitrary asymptotically convergent smooth solutions automatically have finite energy is included.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: The tori and their generators avoid $\Delta$: distinct coordinates of a tuple on a given product torus lie on distinct disjoint attaching curves. The set $u^{-1}(\Delta)$ is a finite set of interior points. Indeed, in local symmetric-function coordinates the repeated-root condition is the vanishing of the polynomial discriminant, a holomorphic defining function, possibly with singular zero set. Near each inverse image of $\Delta$, the equation is the ordinary $J_0$ holomorphic equation because $J_t=J_0$ on $V$. Its discriminant composition is therefore holomorphic. By [F1], its zeros are isolated unless it vanishes on a neighborhood. The set of strip-interior points having a neighborhood mapped into $\Delta$ is open and closed: at a limit point a local discriminant function and [F1] force local vanishing. Connectedness and the boundary condition exclude that possibility. Thus all inverse images are isolated. Uniform end limits exclude sufficiently long strip ends, and compactness of the remaining boundary images excludes a neighborhood of the two strip edges. A closed isolated subset of the resulting compact interior rectangle is finite. [F1, given, construct]

Over the complement of these finitely many points, pull back the $d=m!$ sheeted covering $q:\Sigma^m\setminus q^{-1}(\Delta)\to X\setminus\Delta$. This gives $p:F^\circ\to\mathbb R\times[0,1]$ and a smooth ordered-tuple map $\widetilde u$ with $q\widetilde u=up$. Give $F^\circ$ the complex structure for which $p$ is locally biholomorphic. Complete it across each missing interior point by the following explicit local construction. A finite covering of a punctured disk is described by its monodromy permutation: lift a circle and follow its finitely many sheet labels, splitting them into cycles. A cycle of length $r$ is filled by one disk on which $p(\zeta)=\zeta^r$. Near such a point the original map $u$ is $J_0$ holomorphic. In disjoint coordinate disks about its limiting tuple entries, the lifted coordinates are holomorphic roots off the center, by [F1]; they remain in those bounded disks and extend holomorphically by [F1]. Their symmetric functions continue to equal those of $up$ by continuity. This constructs a smooth branched cover $p:F\to\mathbb R\times[0,1]$ of degree $d$, with a smooth lift $\widetilde u:F\to\Sigma^m$, holomorphic over $u^{-1}(V)$. It also extends continuously at the finitely many ends, since the limiting tuples are off $\Delta$. The monodromy description follows by lifting radial segments after cutting a punctured disk along one radius; the only identification of the resulting sheet copies is the finite permutation across the cut. No compactness theorem for holomorphic maps is used. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

Choose a smaller neighborhood $V_0$ of $\Delta$ with $\overline V_0\subset V$. If $\Delta$ is empty take $V_0=\varnothing$. On the compact set $X\setminus V_0$ the path uniformly tames $\omega$: this is given outside $V$, and on $V\setminus\Delta$ it follows from $J_t=J_0$ and the positive product form. Compactness of the unit tangent bundle over that set, together with compactness of the parameter interval, supplies $c>0$ such that for every relevant tangent vector $a$, $\frac12(|a|_g^2+|J_ta|_g^2)\le c\omega(a,J_ta)$. Consequently the energy integral of $u$ on $u^{-1}(X\setminus V_0)$ is bounded by $c/d$ times the integral of $\widetilde u^*\Omega$ over its preimage in $F$, by the covering change of variables. The equality disregards only finitely many branch points, which have measure zero. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra]

On $p^{-1}(u^{-1}(V_0))$ the map $\widetilde u$ is holomorphic for the product structure. Give $\Sigma^m$ its product Hermitian metric from $(j,\eta)$. Its holomorphic-map energy density equals $\widetilde u^*\Omega$. The smooth map $q$ on compact $\Sigma^m$ has bounded differential into $(X,g)$, so $E_g(q\widetilde u)$ on this part is bounded by a fixed constant times the product energy of $\widetilde u$ there. Conformal invariance of two-dimensional Dirichlet energy gives $E_g(up)=dE_g(u)$ on inverse images of subsets: off the branch points this is the ordinary change of variables with the scalar conformal factor of $p$, which cancels between the inverse metric and the area element. Thus this part has the same type of bound as step 3.1. Both lifted area integrands are nonnegative, by holomorphicity here and by tameness in step 3.1. Combining them gives $$E_g(u)\le\frac{C}{d}\int_F\widetilde u^*\Omega.$$ The lifted map has finite energy: on the tails and away from branch neighborhoods the inverse sheets of $q$ have uniformly bounded differentials, while on finitely many compact branch neighborhoods the constructed lift is smooth. Thus the individual signed area integrals below are absolutely integrable. [step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra]

Write $f_l=\operatorname{pr}_l\widetilde u$. For each region $R$, $f_l:f_l^{-1}(R)\to R$ is proper: its boundary and limiting end values lie on attaching curves, so inverse images of compact subsets of $R$ stay in a compact subset of the completed source away from its boundary and ends. Each component of its domain is a surface without boundary, and the restriction to that component is proper as well. For any compactly supported two-form on $R$, its inverse image is compact and hence meets only finitely many of these open components. Apply [F2] to those components and sum their degree formulas. All nonzero-degree components are among finitely many components: each contains a preimage of any common regular value, since its nonzero signed count is independent of that value, and a proper regular fibre is finite. Therefore there is one integer $d_{l,R}$, the total signed count at a regular value, such that $\int_{f_l^{-1}(R)}f_l^*\beta=d_{l,R}\int_R\beta$ for all compactly supported two-forms $\beta$ on $R$. Exhaust $R$ by compactly supported cutoffs in $\eta$. Absolute integrability from step 4.1 permits passage to the limit, yielding $$\int_{f_l^{-1}(R)}f_l^*\eta=d_{l,R}\int_R\eta.$$ [F2, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Choose a common regular point $p\in R$ for the finitely many coordinate maps, avoiding the finitely many tuple entries at branch values. At an intersection of $u$ with $E_p=\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$ the tuple is then off $\Delta$, so precisely one of its entries equals $p$. Each of its $d$ ordered lifts contributes one preimage of $p$ among the $f_l$, with the same orientation sign: $q$ is a local holomorphic diffeomorphism off $\Delta$, and the normal coordinate to $E_p$ is exactly that entry's local complex coordinate. Consequently $$\sum_l d_{l,R}=d\,n_R(u).$$ In particular this signed multiplicity is independent of the generic point within $R$, and agrees with the disk-domain intersection convention. The inverse image of the attaching curves contributes zero to the integral of each $f_l^*\eta$: at points where $df_l$ has rank below two the pulled-back two-form vanishes, while at rank-two points the inverse function theorem identifies this inverse image locally with a finite union of smooth arcs and their intersection points, a measure-zero set. A countable chart cover retains measure zero. Summing the region formulas in step 5.1 therefore gives $$\int_F\widetilde u^*\Omega=\sum_{l,R}d_{l,R}\int_R\eta=d\sum_R n_R(u)\int_R\eta.$$ Combine this with step 4.1 to obtain the asserted energy bound, whose constant depends only on the fixed metrics, taming bounds, and path. Fixing the domain fixes its right-hand side and proves the final assertion. [F2, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

Assume Countable Choice. Let $e$ be a nonnegative $C^2$ real function on a neighborhood of the closed disk $\overline B_r(0)\subset\mathbb R^2$, where $r>0$. Let $a,b\ge0$ and suppose
$$\Delta e\ge-ae^2-be,\qquad br^2\le1,\qquad a\int_{B_r(0)}e<\frac{3\pi}{64}.$$
Then
$$e(0)\le\frac{16}{3\pi r^2}\int_{B_r(0)}e.$$
The small-energy condition is automatic when $a=0$. Translation gives the identical assertion for a disk centered at any point. This is a scalar differential-inequality estimate; identifying its hypotheses for a holomorphic-map energy density is a separate step.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: If $e(0)=0$, the result follows from $E\ge0$. Otherwise the continuous function $(r-|z|)^2e(z)$ attains a positive maximum at some point $z_0$ with $|z_0|<r$, since it vanishes on the boundary. Set $M=e(z_0)>0$ and $d=(r-|z_0|)/2>0$. For $|z-z_0|\le d$, the inequalities $r-|z|\ge d$ and maximality give $e(z)\le4M$. At the original center maximality also gives $r^2e(0)\le4d^2M$. The closed disk $\overline B_d(z_0)$ lies in the original open disk. [given, construct, algebra]

On this smaller disk $\Delta e\ge-16aM^2-4bM$. Put $K=16aM^2+4bM$. The function $e(z)+K|z-z_0|^2/4$ has nonnegative Laplacian. Applying [F1] to a radius $0<\rho\le d$ and using the disk average of $|z-z_0|^2$, which is $\rho^2/2$, gives $$M\le\frac{1}{\pi\rho^2}\int_{B_\rho(z_0)}e+\frac{K\rho^2}{8}=\frac{1}{\pi\rho^2}\int_{B_\rho(z_0)}e+M(2aM+b/2)\rho^2.$$ Write $q=8aM+2b$, so the last term is $Mq\rho^2/4$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

If $qd^2\le1$, including $q=0$, choose $\rho=d$ in step 2.1. It gives $3M/4\le E/(\pi d^2)$, hence $Md^2\le4E/(3\pi)$. The center comparison from step 1.1 then proves $e(0)\le16E/(3\pi r^2)$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, cases, algebra]

It remains to exclude $qd^2>1$. Since $d\le r/2$ and $br^2\le1$, we have $bd^2\le1/4$. Thus $8aMd^2>1-2bd^2\ge1/2$, so $a>0$ and $M>1/(16ad^2)$. Consequently $b/M\le16abd^2\le4a$, and $q/M=8a+2b/M\le16a$. Choose $\rho=q^{-1/2}<d$ in step 2.1. It yields $$E\ge\int_{B_\rho(z_0)}e\ge\frac{3\pi M}{4q}\ge\frac{3\pi}{64a},$$ contradicting the assumed strict inequality $aE<3\pi/64$. Therefore the case of step 3.1 always holds. The zero-center case in step 1.1 and the same calculation after translation prove every asserted clause. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, cases, algebra] ∎

Let $(X,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold without boundary, and let $J(s,t,x)$ be a smooth family of almost complex structures on $X$, defined for $(s,t)$ in an open subset $U\subset\mathbb R^2$. Suppose the norms of $J$ and its derivatives through total order two, using the Levi-Civita connection in $X$ and ordinary derivatives in $s,t$, are uniformly bounded. Then there are constants $a,b\ge0$, depending only on these bounds and $g$, such that every smooth solution
$$u_s+J(s,t,u)u_t=0$$

$$|du(z)|_g^2\le\frac{32}{3\pi r^2}\int_{B_r(z)}e.$$

$$\Delta e\ge-Ae^2-Be,\qquad \partial_\nu e=-e_t\le ce^{3/2}+de,$$
where $A,B,c,d\ge0$. Put $H=\max\{16A,4096c^2,1\}$. If
$$Br^2\le\frac14,\qquad dr\le\frac1{16},\qquad E:=\int_{B_r^+}e<\frac{\pi}{8H},$$
then
$$e(0,0)\le\frac{16}{\pi r^2}E.$$
No condition on the normal derivative at the curved edge is required. This is a scalar estimate with the flat-boundary measure term retained; deriving the differential inequalities for a map is a separate obligation.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: Reflect the density evenly, $\widehat e(s,t)=e(s,|t|)$, on the full disk. It is continuous and piecewise $C^2$. Distributional integration by parts in the upper and lower half-planes gives $$\Delta\widehat e=(\Delta e)^{\mathrm{even}}+2e_t(s,0+)\,\delta_{\{t=0\}},$$ where $\delta_{\{t=0\}}$ denotes integration along the flat line. Indeed the jump of the first $t$ derivative is $e_t(s,0+)-(-e_t(s,0+))=2e_t(s,0+)$. Thus the atom is bounded below by $-2(c e(s,0)^{3/2}+de(s,0))\delta_{\{t=0\}}$. Its sign is not discarded. The reflected integral is $\int_{B_r}\widehat e=2E$. [given, construct, algebra]

We shall use [F1] also for continuous distributionally subharmonic functions. Here is the needed extension. On any relatively compact disk convolve the continuous function with a nonnegative smooth unit-integral bump supported in a radius-$\varepsilon$ disk. Such bumps are obtained by normalizing $\exp(-1/(1-|x|^2))$ on the unit disk and scaling. Positivity of the distributional Laplacian gives nonnegative ordinary Laplacian after convolution, since its value is the distribution evaluated on a translated nonnegative bump. Apply [F1] on disks whose closed $\varepsilon$ neighborhood remains in the domain. Uniform continuity on compact subsets makes the convolutions converge uniformly to the original continuous function, so their mean-value inequalities pass to the limit. This proves the stated extension without assuming that a reflected function is $C^2$. [F1, construct]

If $e(0,0)=0$, the conclusion follows from $E\ge0$. Otherwise maximize $(r-|z|)^2\widehat e(z)$ on the full closed disk, and let $z_0=(s_0,t_0)$ be a point of positive maximum. Put $M=\widehat e(z_0)>0$ and $\ell=(r-|z_0|)/2$. Maximality gives $\widehat e\le4M$ on $\overline B_\ell(z_0)$ and $r^2 e(0,0)\le4\ell^2M$. On this smaller disk the bulk Laplacian is at least $-K$, with $K=16AM^2+4BM$, and its line atom is at least $-2L\delta_{\{t=0\}}$, with $L=8cM^{3/2}+4dM$. Consequently $$F(z)=\widehat e(z)+K|z-z_0|^2/4+L|t|$$ is distributionally subharmonic there, since $\Delta|t|=2\delta_{\{t=0\}}$. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

Apply step 1.2 to $F$ on a radius $0<\rho\le\ell$ about $z_0$; the endpoint radius follows by continuity if needed. The average of $|z-z_0|^2$ is $\rho^2/2$, and $\bigl||t|-|t_0|\bigr|\le\rho$ there. If $\rho<\ell$, one of the nonlinear terms determines the minimum, so $M\rho^2$ equals $1/(16A)$ or $1/(4096c^2)$, or their common minimum when both are present. In all cases $M\rho^2\ge1/H$. If both nonlinear coefficients vanish, the minimum defining $\rho$ is already $\ell$; the same argument applies. Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a compact smooth manifold without boundary, with a background Riemannian metric $g_0$, and let $L\subset X$ be a compact embedded submanifold without boundary of half its real dimension. Let $J(s,t,x)$ be a smooth uniformly $C^2$ bounded family of almost complex structures for parameters in a neighborhood of a closed upper half-disk. Suppose $J(s,0,x)=J_b(x)$ for $x\in L$, independently of $s$, where $TL\cap J_bTL=0$.

There is a smooth Riemannian metric $g$ on $X$, depending only on $g_0,L,J_b$, such that $J_b$ is orthogonal and $J_bTL$ is perpendicular to $TL$ along $L$. For this metric there are constants $r_0,\varepsilon_0>0$ depending only on the geometric data and uniform family bounds with the following property. If $0<r\le r_0$ and a smooth map $u:\overline B_r^+\to X$ solves $u_s+J(s,t,u)u_t=0$, maps the flat edge into $L$, and satisfies $E=\int_{B_r^+}e_g<\varepsilon_0$, then
$$|du(0,0)|_g^2\le\frac{32}{\pi r^2}E,\qquad \sup_{B_{r/2}^+}|du|_g^2\le\frac{128}{\pi r^2}E,$$
where $e_g=(|u_s|_g^2+|u_t|_g^2)/2$. Uniformly equivalent estimates with constants depending on the data hold for $g_0$. No assumption that the whole image lies in one coordinate chart is made.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: Along $L$ the direct sum $TX|_L=TL\oplus J_bTL$ is smooth, by the dimension and total-reality assumptions. Write vectors uniquely as $a+J_bb$ with $a,b\in TL$, and put $$g_L(a+J_bb,c+J_bd)=g_0(a,c)+g_0(b,d).$$ This is a smooth positive definite form, and $J_b(a+J_bb)=-b+J_ba$ shows that it is $J_b$ orthogonal and that the two summands are perpendicular. Extend this form to a global smooth metric as follows. In adapted submanifold charts, extend its matrix coefficients constantly in the normal coordinates, shrinking each chart to keep positivity. Choose finitely many smaller charts covering compact $L$, with nonnegative smooth bumps $\eta_i$ supported in the larger charts and positive on the smaller ones; each bump is constructed in Euclidean coordinates. Let $\psi=\sum_i\eta_i$ and choose a smooth $\chi$ equal to one near $L$ and supported where $\psi>0$. Such a $\chi$ is a scalar smooth function of $\psi$, since $\psi$ has a positive minimum on $L$. If $g_i$ are the local extensions, set $$g=(1-\chi)g_0+\sum_i\frac{\chi\eta_i}{\psi}g_i,$$ extending the summands by zero away from their supports. This is a smooth convex combination of positive metrics and agrees with $g_L$ on $L$. Only finitely many charts and bumps are chosen. [given, construct, algebra]

Use the pullback Levi-Civita connection of $g$. On the flat edge put $v=u_s\in TL$, so $u_t=J_bv$ and $e_g=|v|_g^2$. Since $J(s,0,x)$ is fixed in $s$ on $L$, $\partial_sJ=0$ there. Moreover $
abla_vJ$ is skew-adjoint at the edge: the identity $\langle Ja,bangle+\langle a,Jbangle=0$ holds along $L$ for arbitrary ambient vectors, and differentiating it in the tangent direction $v$ using metric compatibility gives that assertion. In particular $\langle(
abla_vJ)v,vangle=0$. Torsion-freeness and differentiation of $u_t=Jv$ give $$

abla_su_s,vangle$ on the edge. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

Differentiate the actual density in the normal coordinate $t$. The product rule gives $$

Uniform $C^2$ bounds persist for this metric because on the compact target it and its connections differ from the fixed background data by bounded smooth tensors. We obtain $\Delta e_g\ge-Ae_g^2-Be_g$ throughout the half-disk. Assume Countable Choice. Let $G$ be the unit disk in $\mathbb R^2$ or its upper half-disk. Let $Q\subset\mathbb C^m$ be compact and let $J(s,t,x)$ be smooth on a neighborhood of $\overline G\times Q$, with $J^2=-I$ and uniform bounds on derivatives of every order. Suppose a smooth map $u:\overline G\to Q$ satisfies
$$u_s+J(s,t,u)u_t=0,\qquad \sup_G(|u|+|du|)\le M,\qquad \sup_G\|J(s,t,u)-i\|\le\frac12.$$
In the half-disk case additionally suppose $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$. Then for each $0<\rho<1$ and integer $k\ge0$ there is a uniform bound
$$\|u\|_{H^k(G\cap B_\rho)}+\sup_{G\cap B_\rho}|D^ku|\le C_k.$$
The constants depend only on $m,M,\rho,k$ and finitely many of the indicated coefficient bounds. The estimates apply to already smooth solutions; they do not assert weak-solution regularity.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: We first record the elementary two-dimensional inequalities used in the proof. For a smooth compactly supported vector function $f$ on $\mathbb R^2$, the one-dimensional fundamental theorem gives $|f(s,t)|^2\le2\int_{\mathbb R}|f f_s|(r,t)dr$ and the analogous bound in the other coordinate. Multiply these inequalities and integrate to obtain $$\|f\|_4^4\le4\|f\|_2^2\|f_s\|_2\|f_t\|_2\le2\|f\|_2^2\|\nabla f\|_2^2.$$ Applying the fundamental theorem twice to $|f|^2$ also gives $$|f(s,t)|^2\le2\int_{\mathbb R^2}(|f f_{st}|+|f_s f_t|)\le2\|f\|_2\|f_{st}\|_2+2\|f_s\|_2\|f_t\|_2\le C\|f\|_{H^2}^2.$$ These yield local $H^1\to L^4$ and $H^2\to L^\infty$ bounds after multiplication by a scalar cutoff. They hold on half-disks too, away from the curved edge. For $H^1$ reflect evenly across the flat edge. For $H^2$ extend a compactly supported upper-half-plane function to negative $t$ by $F(s,-t)=3f(s,t)-2f(s,2t)$, $t>0$. Its value and first normal derivative match at zero, so the extension is $C^1$, piecewise smooth, has weak second derivatives with no line atom, and has controlled $H^2$ norm. The first calculation remains valid for the continuous, piecewise smooth even extension, which is absolutely continuous on coordinate lines; the second remains valid for the order-two extension because its value and first derivatives match. [given, construct, algebra]

For $D_0=\partial_s+i\partial_t$ and a smooth compactly supported $w$ on the plane one has $\|D_0w\|_2^2=\|w_s\|_2^2+\|w_t\|_2^2$. Indeed the integrated cross term is zero by integration by parts in both coordinates. The same identity holds on the upper half-plane for compactly supported smooth $w$ whose flat-edge values are real: the remaining flat-boundary cross term is the imaginary part of the pairing of the real vectors $w_s$ and $w$, hence zero. Let $w$ satisfy $D_0w=(i-J)w_t+F$ on a patch, with this boundary condition when needed, and let $\chi$ be a real cutoff compactly supported away from the curved edge. Apply the identity to $\chi w$ and commute the cutoff through the equation. The principal coefficient bound gives $$\|\nabla(\chi w)\|_2\le\tfrac12\|\nabla(\chi w)\|_2+C_\chi\|w\|_2+\|\chi F\|_2,$$ so its first term absorbs. This proves the local first-order estimate on any smaller disk or half-disk, with constants depending on the cutoff margin. [given, construct, algebra]

We prove uniform local $H^k$ bounds by induction, using slightly nested radii between $\rho$ and one. The $H^1$ bound follows from the given $C^1$ bound and the bounded area. Differentiate the equation once in $s$ and put $w=u_s$. Then $$D_0w=(i-J)w_t-(\partial_sJ+(d_xJ)u_s)u_t.$$ Its forcing is bounded in $L^2$ by the given $C^1$ and coefficient bounds. In a half-disk $w$ has real flat-edge values. Step 1.2 therefore bounds $u_{ss}$ and $u_{st}$ on a smaller patch. The equation rewritten as $u_t=Ju_s$ gives $$u_{tt}=(\partial_tJ+(d_xJ)u_t)u_s+Ju_{st},$$ which bounds the remaining second derivative. Thus $u$ has a uniform local $H^2$ bound. Differentiating twice in $s$ gives the same estimate for $u_{ss}$: its commutator terms contain at most one second derivative of $u$, multiplied by bounded first derivatives, and bounded products of first derivatives. These terms are controlled by $H^2$ and $C^1$. Recovering the other third derivatives from $u_t=Ju_s$ proves the $H^3$ bound. [step 1.2, given, algebra]

For the general induction assume the local $H^k$ bound, $k\ge3$, on a slightly larger patch. Differentiating $k$ times in $s$ gives $$D_0(\partial_s^k u)=(i-J)\partial_t\partial_s^k u+F_k.$$ Repeated chain and product rules express $F_k$ as finitely many products of bounded coefficient derivatives and derivatives of $u$ of orders at most $k$, with sum of their orders at most $k+1$; the sole order-$k+1$ term was separated as the principal term. For $k=3$, the only product not directly bounded by the $C^1$ bound times an $H^3$ norm has two second derivatives, which are $L^4$ by step 1.1 applied to the $H^3$ bound. Their product is $L^2$. For $k\ge4$, derivatives of orders at most $k-2$ are locally bounded by step 1.1. A factor of order $k$ can only be accompanied by total derivative order at most one, and a factor of order $k-1$ by total order at most two; in either case put that high-order factor in $L^2$ and the remaining factors in $L^\infty$. There cannot be two factors of order $k-1$, since $2k-2>k+1$ for $k\ge4$. If all factors have orders at most $k-2$, they are bounded and their product is $L^2$ on the finite patch. This controls every term of $F_k$. Step 1.2 now bounds the derivatives of $\partial_s^k u$, with real boundary values retained. To recover an order-$k+1$ derivative with at least two $t$ derivatives, differentiate $u_t=Ju_s$ $k$ times. Its principal term has one fewer $t$ derivative than the derivative on the left, and all other terms are controlled by the same product argument using derivatives through order $k$. Induction on the number of $t$ derivatives bounds them all. This completes the Sobolev induction. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

For each requested derivative order $j$, obtain the $H^{j+2}$ bound on a slightly larger patch from the preceding Sobolev induction. Multiply each $D^ju$ by a cutoff and use the $H^2\to L^\infty$ estimate of step 1.1, including its explicit half-plane extension when needed. This bounds $\sup|D^ju|$ on the desired smaller patch. For any fixed $k$ only finitely many nested radii and coefficient derivatives are used; their constants depend solely on the data stated. All differentiations are of given smooth solutions, so no weak regularity or hidden choice-dependent elliptic theorem has been invoked. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

Let $S=\mathbb R\times[0,1]$, let $(X,g_0)$ be compact without boundary, and let $L_0,L_1\subset X$ be compact embedded submanifolds without boundary, of half the real dimension of $X$. Suppose smooth almost complex families $J_n(s,t,x)$ have uniform bounds for all derivatives on $S\times X$, converge in $C^\infty$ on compact subsets to $J_\infty$, and satisfy $J_n(s,j,x)=J_{b,j}(x)$ for $x\in L_j$, $j=0,1$, independently of $n,s$. Suppose $TL_j\cap J_{b,j}TL_j=0$.

Let $u_n:S\to X$ be smooth up to the boundary, with $u_n(s,j)\in L_j$, satisfying $(u_n)_s+J_n(s,t,u_n)(u_n)_t=0$, and with $g_0$-energies at most $E_0<\infty$. There is a constant $\varepsilon>0$ depending only on the geometric data and uniform coefficient bounds, a finite set $Z\subset S$ with $|Z|\le\lfloor E_0/\varepsilon\rfloor$, and a subsequence converging in $C^\infty$ on every compact subset of $S\setminus Z$, including one-sided derivatives at its boundary, to a map $u_\infty$. The limit satisfies the $J_\infty$ equation, the indicated boundary conditions, and has energy at most $E_0$ on $S\setminus Z$.

This assertion does not extend the map across $Z$, recover lost energy, construct bubble trees, or describe strip breaking at either noncompact end.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: Choose fixed metrics adapted to $L_0,J_{b,0}$ and $L_1,J_{b,1}$ as in the boundary supplier [F1]. On compact $X$ their energies and gradient norms are uniformly comparable to those of $g_0$. The interior supplier and the two boundary suppliers therefore give one $\varepsilon>0$ and one $r_0>0$, with $r_0<1/4$, such that a $g_0$-energy below $\varepsilon$ on any disk or physical-boundary half-disk of radius at most $r_0$ gives a uniform gradient bound on its half-radius portion, in the metric $g_0$. Interior estimates at all points of that portion follow by applying the center estimate on smaller disks contained in the original one. At $t=1$ reflect $t$ to $1-t$ and replace $J_n$ by $-J_n$, which has the same uniform bounds and the appropriate fixed totally real boundary structure. The constants are uniform in $n,s$ by the hypotheses. [F1, given, construct]

Fix a countable basis of relative strip neighborhoods consisting of rational interior disks and rational-center half-disks along its two physical edges, all of radius at most $r_0$. For each basis member $B$, the energies $E_n(B)$ lie in $[0,E_0]$. Pass to one subsequence on which all these numbers converge. This is an explicit countable diagonal extraction: for a bounded real sequence, repeatedly retain the first closed dyadic interval containing infinitely many remaining terms and take least remaining indices; use that deterministic extraction for the first basis member, then the second, and so on, finally taking the diagonal. Write $e(B)$ for the resulting limit and put $$Z=\{p\in S:e(B)\ge\varepsilon\text{ for every basis member }B\ni p\}.$$ If $p_1,\ldots,p_N$ are distinct points of $Z$, choose pairwise disjoint basis neighborhoods around them. Their limiting energies are each at least $\varepsilon$, whereas their sum is at most $E_0$, since the corresponding finite sums of energies of $u_n$ have that bound. Thus $N\varepsilon\le E_0$. It follows that $Z$ is finite with the asserted cardinality bound. Only finitely many neighborhoods are chosen in this last argument. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

For $p\notin Z$, choose a basis neighborhood $B\ni p$ with $e(B)<\varepsilon$. Its actual energies are below $\varepsilon$ for all sufficiently large indices. Choose a smaller disk or physical-boundary half-disk about $p$ whose closure lies in $B$. Step 1.1 bounds the gradients uniformly on a neighborhood of $p$. Finite subcovers give uniform local $C^1$ bounds on every compact subset of $S\setminus Z$. Compactness of $X$ and these derivative bounds give a further subsequence converging locally uniformly to a continuous $u_\infty$. To make the selection precise under Countable Choice, fix finite $2^{-k}$ nets of $X$ for all positive integers $k$, using Countable Choice once for this family, and a countable dense set of source points outside $Z$. At each such point use the fixed nets to extract a convergent subsequence by retaining the first net ball containing infinitely many remaining values, with radii tending to zero, and then least indices; diagonalize over the source points. One may instead use successive finite intersections of the previously retained value sets, so the centers need not form nested balls: their radii tending to zero makes the retained values Cauchy. Local equicontinuity and completeness of compact $X$ extend the dense-point limits uniquely and give uniform convergence on compact subsets, by finite source nets. Thus no arbitrary family of pointwise choices or dependent-choice axiom is needed. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, construct]

Higher bounds can now be obtained in genuine target charts. At an interior source point choose a target chart about its limiting image and make one constant linear coordinate change taking the limiting complex structure at that point to $i$. Local uniform convergence, uniform first-derivative bounds, and convergence of $J_n$ show that on a sufficiently small source disk all large-index images lie in one relatively compact coordinate set and the transformed coefficient differs from $i$ by at most $1/2$. At a boundary point first take an adapted target chart in which $L_j$ is real and the fixed boundary structure is $i$ along it. Here is its construction: in arbitrary target coordinates write $x\mapsto\ell(x)$ for a local parametrization of $L_j$ and set $$F(x,y)=\ell(x)+\sum_{a=1}^m y_aJ_{b,j}(\ell(x))\partial_{x_a}\ell(x).$$ Its derivative at $y=0$ maps the real and imaginary coordinate vectors to a tangent basis and its $J_{b,j}$ image. Total reality makes it invertible; [F3] gives a smooth local inverse. Consequently $F^{-1}$ sends $L_j$ to the real plane and intertwines $J_{b,j}$ with $i$ along it. At the upper strip edge use the reflected structure from step 1.1. Uniform convergence then gives the same coefficient smallness and bounded image in a fixed chart on a small half-disk. All transformed coefficient derivatives are uniformly bounded on these patches, and the coordinate first derivatives of the maps are bounded by step 3.1. [F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Apply [F2] on every patch of step 4.1. It gives uniform bounds for every derivative on smaller patches. Choose a countable such patch cover, possible by second countability of the strip and Countable Choice for witnessing patches. Extract one subsequence on which coordinate derivatives of every order converge locally uniformly on all these patches: use a countable dense set in each patch, bounded finite-dimensional derivative values, the deterministic bounded-sequence extraction of step 2.1, and diagonalize over patches and multi-indices. Uniform bounds of the next derivative give equicontinuity of the derivatives under consideration, so dense-point convergence is locally uniform. Integrating derivatives along coordinate segments shows that the limiting derivative functions are the derivatives of the already determined continuous limit. The limits agree on chart overlaps because their underlying maps converge to the same $u_\infty$ and the smooth coordinate change obeys the chain rule. This proves all the stated local $C^\infty$ convergence, including the half-disk boundary derivatives. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

Pass to the limit in the equation using the $C^1$ convergence of the maps and local $C^\infty$ convergence of the coefficients. Closedness of the compact submanifolds $L_j$ preserves the boundary condition. On every compact subset of $S\setminus Z$, convergence of first derivatives gives convergence of the energy densities and hence an energy integral at most $E_0$. Exhaust the punctured strip by an increasing sequence of compact subsets; monotone convergence gives total limit energy at most $E_0$. None of these arguments controls what happens at the omitted finite set or at either strip end, so precisely the stated compactness conclusion follows. [step 2.1, step 5.1, given, algebra] ∎

Assume Countable Choice. Use a compact target $(X,g)$, fixed compact totally real boundary submanifolds, and smooth strip equations $J_n$ with uniform bounds of every order, fixed boundary complex structures, and local $C^\infty$ convergence to $J_\infty$. Let smooth solutions $u_n$ have energies at most $E_0$. Suppose $p_n\to p$ in the strip, including its boundary, and $|du_n(p_n)|_g\to\infty$.

After taking a subsequence, translations and positive conformal dilations about points tending to $p$ give a nonconstant smooth map $v$ on either $\mathbb C$ or the closed upper half-plane, satisfying the autonomous equation $v_s+J_\infty(p,v)v_t=0$, with energy at most $E_0$. In the half-plane case its real-axis boundary lies in the boundary submanifold at $p$. Its derivative has norm one at some finite point, and its derivative norm is at most two everywhere. There is a constant $\hbar>0$ depending only on the uniform geometric data, independent of the sequence, such that $E(v)\ge\hbar$.

At the upper strip edge an orientation-preserving half-plane coordinate is used. No extension of $v$ over infinity, sphere or disk compactification, energy identity, or bubble-tree statement is asserted.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: Choose a flat source coordinate about $p$, centered there, with domain a disk or an upper half-disk. At the lower strip edge use the usual coordinate; at the upper edge use $z\mapsto i-z$, so both coordinates are orientation preserving and preserve the form of the equation. Write $f_n=|du_n|_g$ in this coordinate and $M_n=f_n(p_n)\to\infty$. After a tail, choose radii $$r_n=\sqrt{|p_n-p|+M_n^{-1}}$$ smaller than a fixed coordinate radius. Then $r_n\to0$, $|p_n-p|/r_n\to0$, and $r_nM_n\to\infty$. On the compact disk or half-disk of radius $r_n$ maximize $(r_n-|z|)f_n(z)$, and let $q_n$ be a maximum point. Put $\lambda_n=f_n(q_n)$ and $\delta_n=(r_n-|q_n|)/2$. The maximum is at least $(r_n-|p_n|)M_n$, so $\lambda_n\delta_n\to\infty$, and in particular $\lambda_n\to\infty$. On $B_{\delta_n}(q_n)$ intersected with the physical source half-plane, maximality gives $f_n\le2\lambda_n$. All selected points tend to $p$. [given, construct, algebra]

If $p$ is interior, rescale by $z\mapsto q_n+z/\lambda_n$. The domains contain disks about zero of radii $\lambda_n\delta_n\to\infty$; the rescaled derivatives are at most two there and have norm one at zero. If $p$ is a boundary point, write $h_n=\lambda_n\operatorname{Im}q_n\ge0$. Pass either to $h_n\to\infty$ or to a bounded sequence converging to $h\ge0$. In the first case use the same center rescaling; its boundary recedes to height $-h_n$, so the limit domain is the plane. In the second case rescale about the boundary foot $\operatorname{Re}q_n$, obtaining upper half-plane domains on which the derivative bound holds on expanding disks centered at $ih_n$. Every fixed compact upper-half-plane set eventually lies in these disks, and the derivative norm is one at $ih_n$. The boundary values remain on the original fixed submanifold. In all cases the rescaled almost complex structures converge locally smoothly to $J_*(x)=J_\infty(p,x)$: each positive source derivative gains a factor $\lambda_n^{-1}$ and the unscaled source points tend to $p$. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

These rescaled maps have a subsequence converging smoothly on compact subsets of their limiting plane or half-plane. Here the details of [F2] apply without removing points: the global derivative bound two already gives local equicontinuity everywhere. Compact target finite nets and a countable dense subset of the limiting domain give a locally uniform subsequence. In a small disk about each limiting source point choose the fixed target coordinates of [F2], normalizing $J_*$ to $i$ at the center; at boundary points use its explicit totally real chart. Locally uniform convergence and smooth coefficient convergence then give the coefficient bound $\|J-i\|\le1/2$ and uniform coordinate $C^1$ bounds on a smaller fixed patch. The bootstrap in [F2] gives bounds of every order there. Its countable derivative diagonal construction yields local $C^\infty$ convergence on an exhaustion of the entire limiting domain, including boundary derivatives. Thus no concentration point remains in this selected scale. [F2, step 2.1, construct]

Let $v$ be the limit. The equation and boundary condition pass to the limit. Its derivative norm is one at zero in the plane-center case, and at $ih$ in the bounded-height case: convergence is $C^1$ on a fixed compact neighborhood of those moving points. Its derivative norm is at most two by the same convergence, so it is nonconstant. A translation and dilation of a two-dimensional source preserves Dirichlet energy, since the squared derivative scaling cancels the area scaling. Therefore every compact-region energy of the rescaled maps is at most $E_0$, and passage to the smooth limit followed by exhaustion gives $E(v)\le E_0$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

Finally choose fixed constants $r_*>0$, $\varepsilon_*>0$, and $C_*>0$ giving the interior center and boundary half-radius supremum estimates of [F1] in the metric $g$, uniformly for every possible autonomous limit $J_*$. This is possible from the uniform coefficient bounds and the two fixed boundary structures; decrease $r_*$ below $1/4$ if necessary. If a derivative-norm-one point of $v$ in the plane, or in the half-plane at height at least $r_*/4$, is considered, apply the interior estimate on a radius-$r_*/8$ disk about it. If its half-plane height is below $r_*/4$, apply the boundary supremum estimate on the radius-$r_*$ half-disk centered at its boundary foot. If total energy is at least $\varepsilon_*$ there is already a positive lower bound. Otherwise the relevant small-energy estimate gives $$1\le\frac{64C_*}{r_*^2}E(v).$$ Consequently $$\hbar=\min\{\varepsilon_*,r_*^2/(64C_*)\}>0$$ is a uniform lower bound for the energy of this nonconstant bubble. This proves exactly the asserted plane or half-plane result, without filling its point at infinity. [F1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎
