Assume Countable Choice. Fix $m\ge1$ and $2<p<\infty$. There are constants $\eta_{m,p}>0$ and $C_{m,p}<\infty$ with the following property. Let $w\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C^m)$ have compact support, let $A$ be a bounded measurable real linear endomorphism-valued coefficient with $\|A\|_\infty\le\eta_{m,p}$, and let $f\in L^2\cap L^p$. If
$$D_0w:=w_s+iw_t=Aw_t+f$$
weakly, then $w\in W^{1,p}$ and $\|\nabla w\|_p\le C_{m,p}\|f\|_p$.

The same assertion holds on the upper half-plane if $w$ has compact support in its closure and is continuous there with real boundary values. The coefficient need not be differentiable. In particular, localizing a continuous $W^{1,2}$ map satisfying this equation on a disk or real-boundary half-disk gives local $W^{1,p}$ regularity whenever its localized forcing belongs to $L^2\cap L^p$.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: With Fourier convention $\widehat{\partial_jw}=2\pi i\xi_j\widehat w$, set $$r_s(\xi)=\frac{i\xi_s}{i\xi_s-\xi_t},\qquad r_t(\xi)=\frac{i\xi_t}{i\xi_s-\xi_t}\quad(\xi\ne0).$$ Both symbols are smooth and homogeneous of degree zero, and their first two derivatives are bounded on the unit circle because the denominator there has modulus one. Homogeneity gives the required Mihlin estimates. Let $R_s,R_t$ be their componentwise multiplier operators. By [F1] their $L^p$ norms on the finite-dimensional vector-valued space are bounded by a finite constant $K=K_{m,p}\ge1$, while their $L^2$ norms are at most one since $|r_s|,|r_t|\le1$. For smooth compactly supported $w$, Fourier differentiation gives $w_j=R_jD_0w$. Approximation in $W^{1,2}$ by [F2] proves the same identities for the given weak $w$. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

Choose $\eta_{m,p}=1/(2K)$. The equation and step 1.1 give $$w_t=R_tAw_t+R_tf$$ as an $L^2$ identity. The real linear operator $R_tA$ has norm at most $1/2$ on both $L^2$ and $L^p$. Therefore the geometric series $$\sum_{k\ge0}(R_tA)^kR_tf$$ converges in each of those spaces. Its partial sums belong to their intersection and have identical distributional meanings: the $L^2$ and $L^p$ multipliers agree on that intersection, because common smooth approximations from [F2] converge in both norms and the multiplier is bounded in each. The two limits thus represent the same distribution. Uniqueness of the $L^2$ solution to $(I-R_tA)v=R_tf$ identifies that limit with the already existing derivative $w_t$. Consequently $\|w_t\|_p\le2K\|f\|_p$. The equation then gives $w_s=(A-i)w_t+f\in L^p$ with a uniform bound, proving $\|\nabla w\|_p\le C_{m,p}\|f\|_p$. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

The function itself lies in $L^p$. Take a square $[-R,R]^2$ containing its support. The distributional identity $\partial_sw=w_s\in L^p$, together with Fubini, gives the one-dimensional primitive formula on almost every horizontal line: subtract $\int_{-R-1}^s w_s(r,t)dr$ from $w(s,t)$; its distributional $s$ derivative is zero, so it is a constant. A distribution with derivative zero is constant because it annihilates every integral-zero compact test, each of which is a derivative of a compactly supported test. The vanishing of $w$ before its support makes that constant zero. Thus Holder on each finite horizontal interval gives $\|w\|_p\le(2R+2)\|w_s\|_p$. In particular $w\in W^{1,p}$. This argument requires no general ACL or Morrey theorem. [step 2.1, given, algebra]

In the half-plane case let $C$ denote componentwise complex conjugation and extend $w$ by $\widehat w(s,-t)=Cw(s,t)$ for $t>0$. This is a compactly supported $W^{1,2}$ map on the plane. To verify the boundary claim directly, apply the primitive argument of step 3.1 on almost every vertical line; the continuous boundary values agree with the resulting finite-endpoint primitive limits. Since these values are real, the reflected values match, and integrating by parts on the two sides leaves no line atom. Define $\widehat A(s,-t)=-CA(s,t)C$ and $\widehat f(s,-t)=Cf(s,t)$, preserving their original values for $t>0$. Then $D_0\widehat w=\widehat A\widehat w_t+\widehat f$ weakly, since below the line $D_0\widehat w=C(D_0w)$ and $\widehat w_t=-Cw_t$; continuity again removes any distributional boundary term. The coefficient norm is unchanged. Apply the plane result and restrict back. Both the reflected forcing norm and derivative norm gain the same factor $2^{1/p}$, so the derivative estimate has the same constants. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

For a local equation multiply the solution by a real smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported in a smaller disk or half-disk and extend it by zero. The product obeys $$D_0(\chi w)=A\partial_t(\chi w)+\chi f+(\chi_s+i\chi_t-A\chi_t)w.$$ The cutoff preserves real boundary values, and its forcing has the claimed integrability whenever the displayed localized terms do. The plane or half-plane result proves the local assertion on the region where $\chi=1$. This completes the weak regularity statement, without assuming differentiability of $A$ or regularity of the weak solution beyond the stated hypotheses. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

$$|f(x)-f(y)|\le C_{p,V}|x-y|^\alpha\|\nabla f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^2)}.$$
The same holds on the closed upper half-plane, with its gradient norm and a possibly larger constant. On a disk $B_{2r}$, or upper half-disk $B_{2r}^+$ including its straight boundary, a $W^{1,p}$ map has a continuous representative on the smaller closed disk or half-disk and satisfies

Assume Countable Choice. Let $G$ be a disk or an upper half-disk in $\mathbb R^2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^{2m}$ be open, and let $J(s,t,x)$ be smooth, including the straight source boundary in the half-disk case, with $J^2=-I$. Let $u:G\to\Omega$ be continuous, belong locally to $W^{1,2}$, and satisfy
$$u_s+J(s,t,u)u_t=0$$
weakly. In the half-disk case assume continuity and local $W^{1,2}$ also up to the straight boundary, $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m\subset\mathbb C^m=\mathbb R^{2m}$, and $\mathbb R^m\cap J(s,0,u(s,0))\mathbb R^m=\{0\}$. Then $u$ is smooth locally, including all one-sided derivatives at the straight boundary. Thus a continuous $W^{1,2}$ weak solution in smooth target charts with a flattened totally real boundary has classical smooth regularity. Continuity at a missing puncture is a premise, not a conclusion.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: Work near one source point $z_0$. A constant real target change makes $J(z_0,u(z_0))=i$. At an interior point choose a real basis $e_1,Je_1,\ldots,e_m,Je_m$ successively in this finite-dimensional complex vector space. At a boundary point take a real basis $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ of the boundary plane; total reality makes $e_1,\ldots,e_m,Je_1,\ldots,Je_m$ a basis, and the change sending these vectors to the standard real and imaginary bases preserves the real boundary plane. Continuity of $u$ and smoothness of $J$ then give a disk or half-disk on which $$A(s,t)=i-J(s,t,u(s,t)),\qquad \|A\|_\infty<\min\{\eta_{m,8},\eta_{m,4}\}.$$ The equation becomes $D_0u=A u_t$. After further shrinking its image is in a compact subset of a convex target coordinate ball. All smooth coefficient derivatives are bounded there. Real cutoffs preserve the boundary condition. [given, construct, algebra]

We record the weak calculus used below. For a continuous $W^{1,q}$ map, the chain rule $\partial_j H(z,u)=H_{z_j}(z,u)+H_x(z,u)\partial_j u$ holds for a smooth $H$ with bounded derivatives on its localized image. Indeed, on interior compact subsets mollify $u$: uniform convergence follows from continuity, convergence of derivatives holds in $L^q$, and the classical chain rule passes to distributions by boundedness and uniform convergence of the coefficient derivatives. This gives the formula everywhere in the open half-domain too; its bounds extend to the boundary because the formula has an integrable right side on the full half-domain. The product rule follows by the same argument whenever one factor and the relevant lower derivatives are bounded, or by Holder when the two differentiated factors have conjugate product integrability. Higher chain and product formulas follow inductively once the corresponding lower derivatives have these bounds. Difference quotients obey $\delta_s(fg)=f(s+h,t)\delta_s g+(\delta_s f)g$, and [F2] bounds the quotients by the weak derivatives on a slightly larger patch. These arguments use countably many mollifications and no selection of weakly convergent subsequences. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Apply [F1] with $p=8$ to a real-cutoff localization of $u$. Its forcing is $(\chi_s+i\chi_t-A\chi_t)u$, which is bounded and compactly supported because $u$ is continuous. The localized map is already $W^{1,2}$, and is continuous and real on the physical boundary. Thus $u\in W^{1,8}$ on a smaller patch. Step 2.1 implies $A\in W^{1,8}$ there. For each sufficiently small nonzero tangential shift $h$, put $v_h=\delta_su$ and $A_h(s,t)=A(s+h,t)$. Subtracting the equations gives $$D_0v_h=A_h(v_h)_t+(\delta_s A)u_t.$$ The last term has a uniform $L^4$ bound by Holder and [F2], since its factors have uniformly bounded $L^8$ norms. The local $L^4$ norm of $v_h$ is uniformly bounded by the tangential quotient estimate. Each $v_h$ separately is continuous, real on the boundary, and $W^{1,2}$: it is a difference of translates of a $W^{1,8}$ map divided by a fixed nonzero number. Therefore [F1] with $p=4$ and a fixed cutoff gives uniform $L^4$ bounds for $(v_h)_s,(v_h)_t$ on a still smaller patch; all forcing terms, including cutoff terms, lie in $L^4\cap L^2$ by finite support. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Apply the converse in [F2] to $u_s$ and $u_t$, whose tangential quotients are the uniformly bounded derivatives of $v_h$. It follows that $u_{ss},u_{st}\in L^4$. The original equation equivalently says $u_t=J(s,t,u)u_s$, since $J^2=-I$. Differentiate this weakly in $t$ using step 2.1: $$u_{tt}=(J_t+J_xu_t)u_s+J u_{st}.$$ Here $J_t$ denotes its explicit source derivative. Both first derivatives of $u$ are in $L^8$, so the product term lies in $L^4$; the other terms do too. Thus $u\in W^{2,4}$ locally. By [F3], $u$ is now $C^{1,1/2}$ on smaller patches up to the physical boundary, with bounded first derivatives. In particular its classical tangential boundary derivative is real. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

Suppose inductively $u\in W^{k,4}$ locally for an integer $k\ge2$. By [F3] applied to its derivatives of order at most $k-2$, all derivatives of order at most $k-1$ have continuous bounded representatives on smaller patches. Repeated use of step 2.1 gives $A\in W^{k,4}$, with all its derivatives of order at most $k-1$ bounded. Put $v=\partial_s^{k-1}u$. Its differentiated equation is $$D_0v=A v_t+G,\qquad G=\sum_{a=1}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}{a}(\partial_s^a A)(\partial_t\partial_s^{k-1-a}u).$$ The function $G$ and its weak $s$ derivative lie in $L^4$: in a differentiated product at most one factor has order $k$, which is $L^4$; every other factor has order at most $k-1$ and is bounded. The same reasoning applies to the chain expansion for $A$, since a term containing a derivative of order $k$ contains it only once. The function $v$ is continuous, belongs to $W^{1,4}$, and has real boundary values, being the tangential derivative of order $k-1$ of a $C^{k-1}$ map whose boundary trace is real. [F3, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Take tangential quotients of the last equation: $$D_0(\delta_s v)=A_h\partial_t(\delta_s v)+(\delta_s A)v_t+\delta_sG.$$ The quotient forcing is uniformly $L^4$ on smaller patches: $\delta_sA$ is uniformly bounded by the bounded classical first derivative of $A$, $v_t\in L^4$, and $\delta_sG$ is controlled by $G_s\in L^4$ and [F2]. Also $\delta_s v$ is uniformly $L^4$ by $v_s\in L^4$. For each fixed $h$ it is continuous, real on the boundary, and $W^{1,2}$ on bounded patches, so [F1] and cutoffs give uniform $L^4$ bounds for its first derivatives. The converse in [F2] gives $\partial_s^{k+1}u,\partial_t\partial_s^k u\in L^4$. This supplies the derivatives of total order $k+1$ with zero or one normal derivative. [F1, F2, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

Recover the other derivatives from $u_t=Ju_s$. For a derivative of total order $k+1$ with $b\ge2$ normal derivatives, apply $\partial_s^{k+1-b}\partial_t^{b-1}$ to this equation. The term in which no derivative hits $J$ is $J\partial_s^{k+2-b}\partial_t^{b-1}u$, already known by induction on $b$. In every other product, derivatives of $u$ have order at most $k$, and differentiated coefficient factors have order at most $k$. If a factor has order $k$, it is the only such factor and all others are bounded; otherwise all factors are bounded. Thus all these terms lie in $L^4$ on a bounded smaller patch. For precision, first differentiate the equation only $k-1$ times, by $\partial_s^{k+1-b}\partial_t^{b-2}$, and then take one more weak $t$ derivative. The highest differentiated $u_s$ factor has a known weak $t$ derivative by the induction on $b$; its coefficient $J$ is $C^1$, so the ordinary first-order weak product rule applies. All other factors have the bounded or $L^4$ derivatives just described. This justifies the displayed expansion without multiplying an undefined high-order distribution by a nonsmooth coefficient, and proves the desired derivative exists in $L^4$. Induction on $b$ proves $u\in W^{k+1,4}$. [step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

Starting with step 4.1, steps 5.1 through 7.1 prove local $W^{k,4}$ for every finite $k$, using nested patches inside the original coordinate neighborhood. To obtain a fixed neighborhood for any specified order, choose its finitely many nested patches between that neighborhood and a larger one; no uniform positive loss after infinitely many inductions is needed. Applying [F3] to each derivative then gives classical derivatives of every order, with their continuous extensions to the straight boundary and the usual tangential boundary derivatives. Zeroth and terms with one or two derivatives on only one factor use $H^2\subset L^\infty$; the remaining second-derivative term is bounded by $\|Df\|_4\|Dg\|_4\le C\|f\|_{H^2}\|g\|_{H^2}$ using $H^1\subset L^4$ on the first derivatives. A smooth coefficient with bounded source derivatives through order two acts as a bounded multiplier by the same product formula. [step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

The extension operators commute with the weight, since they reflect only $t$. Multiplication by $w^{-1}$ is bounded on $H^k$, $k\le3$, since $w^{-1}\le1$ and its derivatives are bounded; logarithmic derivatives of $w$ through these orders are bounded as well. Thus $H^k_\delta$ embeds continuously in $H^k$. Applying step 3.1 to $wu$ gives the claimed weighted value bound; for first derivatives use $wD_su=D_s(wu)-\delta\rho'wu$ and $wD_tu=D_t(wu)$, proving both the weighted $C^1$ bound and the derivative estimate. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

We prove the composition bounds first at weak derivative order two. On a norm-bounded set whose images stay in a smaller target ball, the chain rule gives terms $h_zD^2u$, $h_{zz}Du\,Du$, terms with one explicit source derivative and $Du$, and the twice explicit source derivative $h_{ss}$, $h_{st}$ or $h_{tt}$ evaluated at $u$. Thus the formulas and estimates hold for the weak map itself and the composition is continuous. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

Finally $DQ(u)\xi=[h_z(\cdot,u)-h_z(\cdot,0)]\xi$. Step 6.1 applied to the bracket and the product bound give $\|DQ(u)\|\le C\|u\|_{H^2_\delta}$ on a small bounded ball. Assume Countable Choice. Fix compact $(X,g)$, compact transverse boundary submanifolds $L_0,L_1$, and a smooth $J_t$ with fixed totally real boundary structures. Suppose fixed disjoint generator charts about their finite intersection identify the boundaries with $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$ and $J_t$ with $i$ for every $t$. Fix end generators $x_-,x_+$ and $0\le\delta<\pi/2$, using a smooth weight $e^{\delta\rho(s)}$ as in the weighted Sobolev algebra lemma.

There is an actual second-countable separable real Hilbert configuration manifold $\mathcal B_\delta$ of strip maps with these boundary values and ends, constructed as the union of the following local charts. A reference map $u_0$ is smooth, satisfies the boundary condition, and equals $x_\pm$ outside a compact longitudinal interval. Its tangent model is
$$\mathcal X_{u_0}=H^3_\delta(u_0^*TX)\cap\mathcal X^1_{u_0},$$
where $\mathcal X^1_{u_0}$ is the $H^1$ completion of compactly supported smooth tangent sections satisfying $TL_0,TL_1$ on the edges. This is an intersection with the $H^1$ domain, not an asserted $H^3$ closure. Small sections give maps $u=\mathcal E(u_0,\xi)$ for the actual boundary-preserving local addition. All smooth finite-energy $J_t$ strips with these ends belong to this manifold.

The actual Cauchy–Riemann expression $u_s+J_t(u)u_t$ defines a smooth section of the Hilbert bundle with fiber $H^2_\delta(u^*TX)$. In the local-addition trivialization it is a smooth map $\mathcal F_{u_0}:\mathcal X_{u_0}\to H^2_\delta(u_0^*TX)$. On a small norm ball its nonlinear remainder obeys
$$\|\mathcal F(\xi)-\mathcal F(\eta)-D\mathcal F(0)(\xi-\eta)\|_{H^2_\delta}\le C(\|\xi\|_{H^3_\delta}+\|\eta\|_{H^3_\delta})\|\xi-\eta\|_{H^3_\delta}.$$
The constants are uniform for reference families with uniform coefficient/frame derivatives through the orders used in this estimate. Every zero is smooth and has finite energy and the prescribed ends. At each zero the derivative is the actual geometric Fredholm linearization $H^3_\delta\cap\mathcal X^1\to H^2_\delta$, with the same real index as its $H^1\to L^2$ realization, before translation quotient. No universal transversality or gluing is claimed.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: We first extend the algebra statement of [F2] to compositions in $H^3_\delta$. Its $H^3\subset C^1$ bound makes every first derivative bounded. The third-order product terms are $fD^3g$, $D^3f\,g$, $D^2f\,Dg$ and $Df\,D^2g$; each is $L^2$ using a bounded factor. Thus $H^3$ is an algebra. Weighted versions put the weight on one factor, as in [F2]. Third-order chain terms are a bounded coefficient times $D^3u$, $D^2u\,Du$, or three first derivatives, in addition to lower source-order terms. They have the same weighted $L^2$ bounds, putting at most one differentiated factor in $L^2$ and the others in $L^\infty$. The smooth approximation and Taylor proof of [F2] therefore applies verbatim at this order, with source coefficient derivatives through order three, proving smooth $H^3_\delta$ composition and multiplication. A coefficient's nonzero value at zero is treated as a bounded smooth multiplier, or as a fixed $H^3_\delta$ offset when compactly supported in $s$. All coefficient extensions used below have this latter offset property. [F2, construct, algebra]

The pointwise boundary condition for an $H^3$ section is equivalent to membership in the indicated $H^1$ boundary domain. In fixed product-line coordinates, the forward implication from completion to trace follows from the weak endpoint $L^2$ estimate proved in [F2]; a continuous $H^3$ representative with that trace lies in the closed real plane at every boundary point. Conversely cut a boundary-compatible $H^3$ section off in $s$ in the $H^1$ norm and split it by a real partition in $t$ into two edge pieces and an interior piece. At the lower edge extend the real part evenly and imaginary part oddly; matching real boundary values make this an $H^1$ extension, as verified by the weak primitive and integration-by-parts argument in [F2]. Convolve with a smooth kernel even in the normal variable. The resulting smooth maps have real boundary values and converge in $H^1$. At the upper edge rotate its line to the real line first, reflect about $t=1$, and use the same construction; its piece is supported away from the other edge. The interior piece is convolved away from both edges. Their sum is a compactly supported smooth boundary-compatible approximation in $H^1$. For the variable product planes from [F3] use its smooth scalar gauge first and undo it after approximation. This proves precisely the required $H^1$ membership, without identifying an $H^3$ closure or imposing normal traces. Scalar weights preserve these pointwise planes. [F2, F3, construct, algebra]

The model spaces are separable Hilbert spaces. Use the smooth frame construction of [F3] for $u_0^*TX$; if desired its operator input can be chosen as $\nabla_s+J_t(u_0)\nabla_t$ for the connection in [F1], which is exactly $D_0$ on the constant flat ends. The frame and scalar gauge have bounded derivatives of every fixed order on a compact core and constant comparisons on the ends. They identify the model with a closed real subspace of ordinary weighted $H^3$: the extra $H^1$ domain is closed there. Multiplication by the smooth weight identifies weighted and unweighted Hilbert norms. For separability, split the strip into countably many unit rectangles. By [F5] finite Fourier sums with rational coefficients on finitely many such blocks are a countable dense subset of $L^2$. The graph $f\mapsto(D^\alpha f)_{|\alpha|\le3}$ embeds $H^3$ isometrically as a closed subspace of a finite sum of such $L^2$ spaces; closedness follows by passing weak derivative identities to $L^2$ limits against tests. A closed subspace of a Hilbert space has its orthogonal projection under Countable Choice: a minimizing sequence exists by that axiom and is Cauchy by the parallelogram identity; its unique limit is the nearest point and the usual orthogonality calculation gives a bounded linear projection. Project the countable ambient dense family to obtain a countable dense family in the graph, and then in the boundary subspace by the same argument. This proves the model assertion without an unrestricted-choice subspace theorem. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

For a small $H^3_\delta$ ball of $\xi\in\mathcal X_{u_0}$, [F2] makes its supremum small enough for [F1], so $u=\mathcal E(u_0,\xi)$ is a well-defined $C^1$ map with boundary in $L_j$. Both its value and first derivative approach the prescribed ends. For $\delta=0$ the decay follows by localizing the $H^3$ norm on unit longitudinal windows: their norms tend to zero on the tails by integrability, and the fixed local embedding bound in [F2] gives uniform $C^1$ decay. For positive weight the same estimate applies, or directly uses its exponential factor. References have constant ends, so the reference derivative is compactly supported. Thus $du\in L^2$ and the map has finite energy. The pointwise inverse local addition identifies the chart injectively. Conversely its coordinate inverse is $H^3_\delta$ whenever a second chart map is sufficiently close in this topology, by step 1.1 and bounded smooth finite-dimensional inverse coefficients. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Charts are smoothly compatible on their overlap. The transition formula is the pointwise expression $\eta=\mathcal E^{-1}_{u_1}(\mathcal E(u_0,\xi))$. Near any overlap map its finite-dimensional formula has uniform positive distance from the boundary of its definition domain. On the compact source core extend its smooth coefficients off that graph by finitely many ordinary smooth coordinate cutoffs; this is possible since the graph is compact and contained in an open coefficient domain. On the ends both references are the same constants and the local addition is linear, so the transition is a fixed linear coordinate change with zero offset. Thus step 1.1 gives a smooth $H^3_\delta$ transition near that map. Its pointwise boundary values lie in $T L_j$ by the inverse assertion of [F1]; by step 1.2 it therefore lies in exactly the other model $H^3_\delta\cap\mathcal X^1$, not a larger unproved domain. Its inverse has the same property. Smoothness restricts to these closed Hilbert subspaces because all derivatives are limits of difference quotients in the respective closed target space. This proves the local Hilbert atlas for the union of these actual chart images. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

A zero gives a continuous weak $W^{1,2}$ solution with totally real boundary, so [F4] makes it smooth up to the boundary. Finite energy and its prescribed ends were proved in step 3.1. Conversely every smooth finite-energy strip has the exponential all-order tails of [F4]. Truncate it sufficiently far out by a real cutoff in the exact product generator coordinates to obtain a smooth reference equal to $x_\pm$ on the ends, preserving both linear boundary planes. The inverse local-addition difference between this reference and the original map tends to zero in $H^3_\delta$ as the truncation moves out, because $\delta<\pi/2$ and the tails decay with that spectral rate. It is pointwise tangent on the boundary and thus belongs to the model by step 1.2. For large truncation the strip therefore lies in that actual chart, proving that all smooth finite-energy strips are included. [F1, F4, step 1.2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

This atlas is second-countable. An explicit finite-atlas embedding of $X$ is $F(x)=(\phi_i(x),\phi_i(x)x_i(x))_i$, where $\phi_i$ is a finite smooth partition in coordinate charts; equality or differential vanishing recovers a point or tangent vector in a chart with $\phi_i>0$. Compactness makes it an embedding. Fix a smooth ambient reference $r(s,t)$ equal to $F(x_\pm)$ outside a compact interval. Map our configuration space into the separable Hilbert space $H^3_\delta(S;\mathbb R^N)$ by $u\mapsto F(u)-r$. The local composition estimates show this is continuous in each chart, injective, and has continuous local inverse on its image. For the last assertion, use the smooth inverse local addition and smooth local inverses of $F$ in finite relatively compact target charts; finite cutoffs give bounded coefficient extensions, so step 1.1 applies. Consequently each chart image is open in the subspace topology of this embedding: nearby configurations have an inverse coordinate close in $H^3_\delta$ and satisfy its boundary domain by step 1.2. A subspace of a second-countable metric space is second-countable, so this topology has a countable base. A countable chart subcover can be selected under Countable Choice by choosing one chart containing each basis element that is contained in some chart. This proves the stated configuration manifold properties. No assertion that every arbitrary pointwise constrained rough map has already been approximated in $H^3$ was used or needed. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Define the range bundle using $\mathcal T_\xi=d_v\mathcal E(u_0,\xi)^{-1}:u^*TX\to u_0^*TX$ and the fixed $H^2_\delta$ target in a chart. This inverse exists for the small sections by [F1]. Its coefficient and its inverse have the bounded smooth composition estimates of [F2]; transition multiplication is consequently a smooth bounded invertible $H^2_\delta$ operator depending smoothly on the $H^3_\delta$ chart variable. These are the actual Hilbert-bundle trivializations. In them the section is $$\mathcal F_{u_0}(\xi)=\mathcal T_\xi\bigl(\partial_s\mathcal E(u_0,\xi)+J_t(\mathcal E(u_0,\xi))\partial_t\mathcal E(u_0,\xi)\bigr).$$ The weak chain rule follows from the same smooth approximation as [F2]. In a smooth bundle frame this is a sum of smooth bounded coefficients in $(s,t,\xi)$ times $\xi_s,\xi_t$, and a zeroth-order term. The zeroth-order value at zero is smooth and compactly supported in $s$, because $u_0$ has constant ends. Its difference from that value vanishes at $\xi=0$. Thus [F2], step 1.1 and bounded differentiation $H^3_\delta\to H^2_\delta$ prove that this is a genuine smooth section in the asserted Hilbert bundle. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

The same formulas give the quadratic bound. Their first and second Frechet derivatives are finite sums of bounded smooth coefficient compositions, variations and first derivatives of variations; multiplication is controlled by the $H^2_\delta$ algebra and $H^3_\delta\to H^2_\delta$ differentiation in [F2]. On a fixed small norm ball the second derivative is bounded by a constant depending only on the finitely many coefficient and frame derivative bounds used there. The fundamental theorem along line segments then gives $$\|D\mathcal F(\zeta)-D\mathcal F(0)\|\le C\|\zeta\|_{H^3_\delta}.$$ Integrating from $\eta$ to $\xi$ gives exactly the displayed remainder estimate. This proof shows uniformity for reference families with the specified uniform bounds, rather than assuming a uniform nonlinear estimate as a moduli axiom. [F2, step 5.2, construct, algebra]

At a zero, differentiation of the section is its actual geometric linearization: in local target coordinates it is $P\xi=\xi_s+J_t(u)\xi_t+(dJ_t)_u[\xi]u_t$. Differentiating the range trivialization adds a factor times the section itself, which vanishes there. The same observation makes coordinate changes conjugate this derivative intrinsically. Far out on either end, the map lies in the fixed generator chart, where $J_t=i$ exactly and its target derivatives vanish, so the operator is exactly $D_0$ with the two product boundary planes. Its smooth coefficients and frames have bounded derivatives of all orders on the compact core and exponentially controlled ends by [F4]. All hypotheses of the actual geometric frame and higher Sobolev Fredholm results in [F3] therefore hold. At this smooth zero the pointwise derivative $d_v\mathcal E$ and its inverse have bounded smooth coefficients; they identify the chart tangent space with the actual geometric section space and carry its boundary tangent plane bijectively to $TL_j$, by differentiating the boundary-preserving local addition. Our domain is therefore exactly their $H^3_\delta\cap\mathcal X^1$, justified in step 1.2, and our range is their $H^2_\delta$. They give the asserted Fredholmness and common real index before translation quotient. This completes the actual configuration-space and section construction while leaving universal submersion and gluing as separate obligations. [F3, F4, step 1.2, step 5.2, step 4.2, construct, algebra] ∎

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: Choose a fixed $S$ so that both tails adjacent to $y$ lie in a common smaller product chart $q$ for $s\ge S$ on $u^-$ and $s\le-S$ on $u^+$. By [F2], every fixed derivative order satisfies $|D^kv^-(s,t)|\le C_ke^{-\pi s/2}$ on the positive tail and $|D^kv^+(s,t)|\le C_ke^{\pi s/2}$ on the negative tail. Let a real smooth cutoff $\chi(s)$ equal one for $s\le-1$ and zero for $s\ge1$. For large $R$ define $u_R$ to equal the two stated translates outside $[-1,1]$, and on that joining region put $$q(u_R)=\chi(s)v^-(s+R,t)+(1-\chi(s))v^+(s-R,t).$$ The smallness of the tails keeps this in the common chart. It is smooth, has the exact two boundary conditions, and is unchanged from its component maps where the cutoff is constant. The entire interval $[-R+S,R-S]$ lies in that same chart after increasing $S$ if necessary. [F2, given, construct, algebra]

Construct fixed component right inverses $Q^\pm:H^2\to H^3\cap\mathcal X^1$. The actual component operators are Fredholm by [F3] and surjective by hypothesis. In an $H^1$ orthogonal complement of their kernels the positive lower bound in [F3] gives a unique bounded inverse to each full $L^2$ range, hence a bounded right inverse $L^2\to H^1$. For $H^2$ inputs the higher regularity estimate in [F3] puts its image in $H^3$ with a bounded norm. Restricting produces the claimed $Q^\pm$. Their boundary condition is exactly the $H^1$ domain intersected with $H^3$, not any unproved stronger closure. They are fixed operators, independent of $R$. [F3, given, construct, algebra]

In this chart $J_t=i$ and the local addition is coordinate addition. The two tail maps solve $D_0v=0$, so the pregluing error has the exact coordinate expression $$\chi'(s)(v^-(s+R,t)-v^+(s-R,t)).$$ It is supported in the fixed-width join and its derivatives through order two are $O(e^{-\pi R/2})$ by step 1.1. This proves the claimed $H^2$ error bound. The maps $u_R$ have uniform derivatives of every fixed order. They have finite energy, uniform derivative Sobolev bounds at every fixed order, and exponentially decaying ends, because they are two translates of fixed smooth component maps plus this small fixed-width join. Truncating their outer ends gives actual constant-end references and puts them in the configuration space of [F1]. The same local-addition chart construction can be centered at $u_R$: its coefficients have the stated uniform bounds and its end offsets are exponentially Sobolev integrable. Thus [F1] applies with a uniform radius and uniform first and second section derivative bounds. The nonlinear derivative Lipschitz bound follows, with one constant $L$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

For clarity fix norms suitable for the matching. Use the boundary-preserving connection of [F1], flat on smaller generator neighborhoods, and a smooth target metric equal to the coordinate Euclidean metric there. Such a metric is obtained by positive finite cutoff interpolation with any original metric; it is uniformly equivalent to $g$. Covariant derivative Sobolev norms of orders through three with this connection and metric are equivalent to the norms of [F1]. On a common generator chart they are exactly the ordinary coordinate norms. Hence identifying a section over one nearby base map with a section over another by equal $q$ coordinates is an isometry of these local derivative norms. Where base maps coincide the identification is the identity. This fixes all domain and target norms and makes their matching constants independent of neck length. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

The linearization $D_R$ matches these two operators exactly on the appropriate halves. On $s\le-1$, the base map is exactly the left translate and the pregluing section vanishes, so its linearization is the corresponding translated component operator; likewise on $s\ge1$ for the right. On the whole common-generator interval from step 1.1 the nonlinear expression is $D_0(q(u_R)+\eta)$, since both the coefficient and local addition are exactly linear there. Thus its derivative is exactly $D_0$, even though the preglued map itself has a small residual in its join. The same is true for the shifted component operators on their ends. Identify bundles on these overlaps by $q$ coordinates and elsewhere by equality of the base maps. These identifications preserve boundary tangent spaces and the exact operator expressions. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

We arrange smooth dependence without claiming operator-norm smoothness of translation on a fixed Sobolev space. The actual map $R\mapsto u_R$ is smooth in the configuration topology: its derivatives differentiate the two fixed translates and the fixed cutoff, and every resulting component derivative has finite Sobolev norm by [F2]. Strong continuity and differentiation of these translations follow by smooth approximation and the fundamental theorem in the longitudinal variable. These derivatives have uniform bounds at each fixed order. The local-addition identifications between $u_R^*TX$ and $u_{R_j}^*TX$ for $R$ close to $R_j$ preserve boundary planes and give smooth norm-bounded maps on $H^3$ and $H^2$. In those fixed spaces the explicit local section formulas in [F1] show that $D_R$ depends smoothly in operator norm, with a uniform local Lipschitz bound. Only pointwise smooth coefficient multiplication and bounded first differentiation occur; no conjugation of an arbitrary bounded operator by norm-differentiable translations is being presumed. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

Choose real cutoffs $\beta_-^R,\beta_+^R$ with $(\beta_-^R)^2+(\beta_+^R)^2=1$, $\beta_-^R=1$ for $s\le-R/4$ and zero for $s\ge R/4$, and $|D_s^k\beta_\pm^R|\le C_kR^{-k}$ for $k\ge1$. For example take cosine and sine of a fixed smooth step from zero to $\pi/2$ evaluated at $s/R$. For large $R$ their transition lies in the exact common-generator interval. Define $P_R$ as follows: multiply a target section by $\beta_-^R$, identify and translate it to the left component, extend by zero where its cutoff vanishes, apply $Q^-$, translate and identify the result back where defined, and multiply by $\beta_-^R$ again; add the identical right construction with $\beta_+^R,Q^+$. Smooth flatness of the cutoffs where they vanish makes the zero extensions legitimate in $H^2$ and $H^3$. The bundle identifications and translations have the norm control of step 2.2, and multiplication by these cutoffs is uniformly bounded through order three. Thus $\|P_R\|_{H^2\to H^3}\le C$. All boundary domains are preserved by the pointwise tangent identifications and real cutoffs. [step 2.2, step 1.2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

The only errors are the outer cutoff commutators $\partial_s\beta_\pm^R$ times the transported component solutions. Their $H^2$ norms are at most $C R^{-1}$ times the $H^3$ norm of those solutions: the product formula differentiates the cutoff at most three times, all bounded by $C/R$ for $R\ge1$. Therefore $\|K_R\|_{H^2\to H^2}\le C/R$. Choose $R$ large enough that this is at most $1/2$ and set $$Q_R^{\rm raw}=P_R(I+K_R)^{-1},\qquad (I+K_R)^{-1}=\sum_{n\ge0}(-K_R)^n.$$ It is an actual right inverse for $D_R$ with a uniform norm $M_0$. This proves surjectivity by construction, without assuming a glued Fredholm estimate. [step 1.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Choose a uniform small parameter radius $a>0$ so that the operator difference in those identifications satisfies $\|D_R-D_{R_j}\|M_0\le1/2$ for $|R-R_j|<a$. [F4, step 2.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra]

Let $g_R=\mathcal E(u_R,\xi_R)$. It is a zero of the actual section, so [F1] makes it smooth with finite energy and the prescribed end generators. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 7.1, construct, algebra]

Assume Countable Choice and the actual regular broken pair, pregluing $u_R$, uniform right inverse $Q_R$, corrected strip $g_R$ and unweighted $H^3\to H^2$ realizations of the actual pregluing-and-correction lemma. Let $D^-,D^+$ be the component operators, $D_R$ the pregluing derivative, and $\widetilde D_R$ the derivative at the corrected zero, written in the same local-addition domain and target charts. Put $K^\pm=\ker D^\pm$.

For large $R$ there are smooth linear isomorphisms
$$\Gamma_R:K^-\oplus K^+\longrightarrow\ker D_R,\qquad \widetilde\Gamma_R:K^-\oplus K^+\longrightarrow\ker\widetilde D_R,$$
with uniformly bounded norms and inverse norms. If $A_R(k^-,k^+)$ is the sum of the two translated kernel sections multiplied by the long cutoffs from the pregluing construction, then
$$\|\Gamma_R k-A_Rk\|_{H^3}+\|\widetilde\Gamma_R k-A_Rk\|_{H^3}\le Ce^{-cR}\|k\|_{H^3\oplus H^3}$$
for uniform $C,c>0$. In particular the actual corrected regular-strip index is the sum of the two actual component indices, before translation quotient. This proves kernel matching, not a collar or exhaustion statement.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: Every component kernel section has uniformly controlled exponentially decaying tails. On an exact generator end its coordinates solve $D_0k=0$ with the two product real planes. Expand them in the real basis of [F3]; coefficients satisfy $a'+\lambda a=0$, $\lambda=\pi n-\pi/2$. The $L^2$ condition kills growing modes on the corresponding end. The surviving absolute eigenvalues are at least $\pi/2$. Their coefficients at a fixed end slice have squared sum bounded by $C\|k\|_{H^1}^2$: the slice $L^2$ norm follows from the fundamental theorem for its square on a unit longitudinal neighborhood and Cauchy-Schwarz. Differentiated Fourier sums, bounded by Cauchy-Schwarz and $\sum\lambda^{2q}e^{-2|\lambda|s}$, then give exponential tails in every fixed derivative and Sobolev norm, with constants linear in $\|k\|_{H^1}$. Higher regularity on the compact core is supplied by [F2]. Thus all estimates are uniform over a norm-bounded set of the finite-dimensional kernels. [F2, F3, construct, algebra]

We record the elementary kernel stability used for the correction. Let two surjective bounded operators $T,U:X\to Y$ have specified right inverses $Q_T,Q_U$, with their norms and the operator norms uniformly bounded. Put $P_T=I-Q_TT$ and $P_U=I-Q_UU$. On $\ker T$, the map $P_U$ differs from the identity in ambient $X$ norm by at most $\|Q_U\|\|U-T\|$; on $\ker U$, $P_T$ differs similarly. Thus $P_TP_U$ on $\ker T$ and $P_UP_T$ on $\ker U$ differ from their identities by at most $C\|U-T\|$. If this is less than one, both have bounded Neumann inverses. It follows that $P_U:\ker T\to\ker U$ is bijective, with inverse supplied by either composition, and has uniformly bounded inverse. This proof uses actual complementary projections and completeness only, not an appeal to dimension equality. [given, construct, algebra]

Define $A_R(k^-,k^+)$ by translating, identifying and multiplying these two sections by the outer cutoffs $\beta_-^R,\beta_+^R$ exactly as in [F1]. It is a uniformly bounded map $K^-\oplus K^+\to H^3$. Exact operator matching gives $$D_RA_Rk=(\partial_s\beta_-^R)k^-_{\rm shifted}+(\partial_s\beta_+^R)k^+_{\rm shifted}.$$ On their transition the component end coordinates are at distance at least $3R/4$ along the respective tails. Step 1.1 and the cutoff derivative bounds therefore give $\|D_RA_Rk\|_{H^2}\le Ce^{-cR}\|k\|$ for some fixed $c>0$. Set $P_R=I-Q_RD_R$ and $\Gamma_R=P_RA_R$. Since $D_RQ_R=I$, this takes values in $\ker D_R$ and differs from $A_R$ by at most $Ce^{-cR}\|k\|$ in $H^3$. All these maps depend smoothly on $R$: on the finite-dimensional kernels translations differentiate fixed smooth exponentially decaying functions, and the remaining operators are the smooth families in [F1]. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Define a uniformly bounded map $S_R:H^3(u_R^*TX)\to K^-\oplus K^+$ as follows. Cut a section by $\beta_-^R$, identify and translate it to the left component and extend by zero as in [F1], then apply $\Pi^-=I-Q^-D^-$; do the corresponding right operation with $\Pi^+$. Each $\Pi^\pm$ is a bounded projection onto its component kernel. When applied to $A_Rk$, the main component is the kernel vector multiplied by the squared corresponding cutoff; the lost far tail is exponentially small by step 1.1. The other component contributes only in the long cutoff overlap, where that component kernel is exponentially small. Thus $$\|S_RA_R-I_{K^-\oplus K^+}\|\le Ce^{-cR}.$$ Since $S_R$, $Q_R$ are uniformly bounded and $D_RA_R$ is exponentially small, also $\|S_R\Gamma_R-I\|\le Ce^{-cR}$. For large $R$ this is less than one, so its Neumann inverse is bounded. Hence $\Gamma_R$ is injective and has a uniform lower norm bound. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

To prove surjectivity, let $\eta\in\ker D_R$ and cut it into component sections $\eta^\pm$ with one cutoff each, exactly as in step 3.1. Exact matching now gives $D^\pm\eta^\pm=(\partial_s\beta_\pm^R)\eta$ in the matching coordinates. Consequently $$\|\eta^\pm-\Pi^\pm\eta^\pm\|_{H^3}=\|Q^\pm D^\pm\eta^\pm\|_{H^3}\le C R^{-1}\|\eta\|_{H^3}.$$ On translating back and multiplying by the outer cutoffs, their squared sum is exactly one, so $$\|\eta-A_RS_R\eta\|_{H^3}\le C R^{-1}\|\eta\|_{H^3}.$$ The operators $P_R$ have a uniform norm, because $Q_R$ and the coefficients of $D_R$ do. Applying $P_R$ and using $P_R\eta=\eta$ yields $\|\eta-\Gamma_RS_R\eta\|\le C R^{-1}\|\eta\|$. The closed Hilbert space $\ker D_R$ is complete; thus $\Gamma_RS_R$ is invertible there by its actual Neumann series for large $R$. Every vector of that kernel is therefore in the image of $\Gamma_R$. Along with step 3.1 this proves the first isomorphism with uniform inverse bound. No index-additivity theorem was assumed. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Apply step 1.2 with $T=D_R$ and $U=\widetilde D_R$. In the fixed pregluing charts the nonlinear derivative estimate in [F1] gives $\|\widetilde D_R-D_R\|\le C\|\xi_R\|_{H^3}\le Ce^{-\pi R/2}$. The corrected Newton right inverse from [F1] is smooth and uniformly bounded. Hence $\widetilde P_R=I-\widetilde Q_R\widetilde D_R$ restricts to an isomorphism $\ker D_R\to\ker\widetilde D_R$, differing from the identity there by $O(e^{-\pi R/2})$. Define $\widetilde\Gamma_R=\widetilde P_R\Gamma_R$. This is the claimed second smooth isomorphism, has uniform norm and inverse bounds, and its difference from $A_R$ obeys the stated exponential estimate by step 2.1. At the corrected smooth solution the local-addition tangent identification is the actual geometric linearization identification proved in [F1], so this is a result about that operator, not only a chart derivative. [F1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

The actual component and corrected operators are surjective Fredholm operators by [F1] and [F2]. Their indices are consequently their kernel dimensions. The isomorphism in step 5.1 gives $$\operatorname{ind}\widetilde D_R=\dim K^-+\dim K^+=\operatorname{ind}D^-+\operatorname{ind}D^+.$$ All indices are before any quotient by longitudinal translation. The construction gives actual kernel matching and a small perturbation comparison; it does not yet identify a nonlinear collar or prove that every solution near the broken pair has the prescribed correction form. [F1, F2, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

Assume Countable Choice and the compact transverse strip geometry with fixed exact all-$t$ product-integrable generator charts used for actual strip pregluing. Let $u^-:x_0\to y$ and $u^+:y\to x_2$ be nonconstant smooth finite-energy $J_t$ strips whose actual geometric $H^1\to L^2$ linearizations are surjective and have real index one, before translation quotient. Use the explicit pregluing $u_R$, local addition, and corrected solutions $g_R$ constructed with a smooth uniformly bounded right inverse. Write $\tau_a u(s,t)=u(s+a,t)$.

The right inverses in that construction can be chosen so that, for all sufficiently large $R_0$, the map
$$\mathbb R\times(R_0,\infty)\longrightarrow\{\text{actual regular strips }x_0\to x_2\},\qquad (a,R)\longmapsto\tau_a g_R$$
is smooth, injective, and a local diffeomorphism onto the actual two-dimensional zero manifold. Thus $R\mapsto[g_R]$ is an injective smooth local coordinate in the translation quotient. The endpoint $R=\infty$ is the broken pair $([u^-],[u^+])$.

It has the following precise exhaustion property. Suppose actual strips $w_n$ admit shifts $c_n^-<c_n^+$ with $c_n^+-c_n^-\to\infty$ and
$$w_n(s+c_n^-,t)\longrightarrow u^-(s,t),\qquad w_n(s+c_n^+,t)\longrightarrow u^+(s,t)$$
smoothly on compact sets. Assume their breaking has exactly these two nonconstant levels and no bubbles or additional energy loss, in the energy-identity and neck-collapse sense of actual bubbled strip compactness. Equivalently for the neck requirement used here, outside large fixed translated component cores, the left tail, middle neck, and right tail lie uniformly close to $x_0,y,x_2$, respectively, with the closeness tending to zero as the core radius tends to infinity. Then, for all sufficiently large $n$, there are unique $a_n\in\mathbb R$ and $R_n>R_0$ with $w_n=\tau_{a_n}g_{R_n}$, and
$$R_n-\tfrac12(c_n^+-c_n^-)\longrightarrow0,\qquad a_n+\tfrac12(c_n^-+c_n^+)\longrightarrow0.$$
Conversely $[g_R]$ converges to this broken pair as $R\to\infty$, with no bubbles or energy loss. Consequently this family, together with its broken endpoint, is a topological one-sided collar for this fixed two-level limit, with a smooth interior. No differentiability at a chosen compactifying parameter is asserted. The statement makes no claim that index hypotheses exclude other bubble or boundary-degeneration strata.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: Put $\epsilon_R=e^{-\pi R/2}$. We first choose the right inverses with uniform bounds on their first two parameter derivatives in the moving bundle coordinates of [F1]. In its construction, the coefficients of $D_R$, the local-addition identifications and their first two $R$ derivatives have uniform bounds: they differentiate translates of fixed smooth component maps, with uniformly bounded derivatives and integrable tails, and a fixed joining cutoff. Fix a parameter radius $a>0$ for the local Neumann formula, uniformly small so its denominator has inverse norm at most two. At arithmetic grid points $R_j$ use the already constructed right inverses of uniform norm. On $|R-R_j|<a$ the formula is $Q_j(R)=Q_j(R_j)[I+(D_R-D_{R_j})Q_j(R_j)]^{-1}$ in the fixed local spaces. Differentiating the Neumann inverse twice gives uniform bounds in terms of the first two coefficient derivatives and the fixed inverse bound. Transfer back using the same bounded smooth bundle identifications. Average these exact right inverses with translates of one fixed parameter bump divided by their locally finite sum. The overlap number and derivatives of this partition are uniformly bounded. Thus $Q_R,Q_R',Q_R''$ are bounded independently of $R$. Replacing the original smooth choice by this specified choice preserves all conclusions of [F1] and [F2]. [F1, F2, F4, construct, algebra]

We record carefully the smoothness of translation on the regular zero manifold. For each integer $k\ge3$, the construction of [F3] extends to $H^k\cap\mathcal X^1\to H^{k-1}$. The normal extension is the same finite reflected linear combination with coefficients satisfying $\sum_j a_j(-j)^\ell=1$ for $0\le\ell<k$, a nonsingular Vandermonde system. It matches precisely the weak derivatives through order $k-1$ and adds no boundary condition. The $H^2$ algebra and $H^k\subset C^{k-2}$ give the higher product bounds: in a derivative of a product of total order $k\ge3$, at most one factor has order greater than $k-2$, so that factor is estimated in $L^2$ and the others in $L^\infty$. The low order $H^2$ case is already [F3]. Taylor's integral formula gives smooth composition and the actual higher chart and section formulas, with the same zeroth boundary trace argument. At any fixed smooth regular zero the higher operator is surjective by [F3], has the same finite-dimensional kernel, and has a bounded right inverse obtained by restricting its $H^1$ inverse and using the higher regularity estimate. Apply [F4] at orders $3$ and $k$. Inclusion of the higher zero chart into the $H^3$ zero chart has derivative the identity on this common kernel. The finite-dimensional inverse theorem, or the contraction proof of [F4] on that finite-dimensional kernel, makes this inclusion a local smooth diffeomorphism. Thus every local smooth family in the $H^3$ regular zero manifold is locally smooth in every $H^k$ topology. Translation of such a family is then smooth into $H^3$: its $a$ derivatives are longitudinal derivatives, and any prescribed finite order is controlled by taking a sufficiently high $k$. The translation difference quotients converge by the fundamental theorem and smooth approximation, as in [F1]. This is a statement on the actual regular zero manifold; it does not assert norm differentiability of translation on all $H^3$ maps. [F3, F4, construct, algebra]

The actual component kernel is spanned by $u_s^\pm$. Translation invariance of the equation gives these kernel sections, their nonzero norm follows from nonconstancy, and their exponential tails put them in every indicated Sobolev realization. Surjectivity and index one make each kernel one-dimensional. Choose smooth compactly supported real test covectors $\psi^\pm$ on the component cores with $\ell^\pm(u_s^\pm)=1$, where $\ell^\pm(k)=\int\psi^\pm(k)$. Explicitly use a nonnegative compact cutoff times the metric dual of $u_s^\pm$, divided by its positive squared integral. Translate these tests to the two cores of $g_R$, using the fixed local-addition identifications, and call their pair $\ell_R$. Its operator norm on geometric $H^3$ is uniform. By [F2] it maps the actual two-dimensional kernel at $g_R$ isomorphically to $\mathbb R^2$, with a uniform inverse bound: on the glued copies of $(u_s^-,0),(0,u_s^+)$ its matrix is $I+O(e^{-cR})$. All harmless tangent identifications between the preglued and corrected maps differ by $O(\epsilon_R)$ on these compact tests. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

We next turn the prescribed no-bubble breaking into global $H^3$ closeness, rather than assuming it. Put $d_n=(c_n^-+c_n^+)/2$, $T_n=(c_n^+-c_n^-)/2$, and $v_n(s,t)=w_n(s+d_n,t)$. Its cores are at $-T_n,+T_n$. Fix a sufficiently large core radius $S$. The assumed smooth convergence makes $v_n$ converge to the corresponding translates of the two components on these fixed-width cores and collars. The neck-collapse part of the hypothesis puts the remaining three regions, for large $S,n$, in the exact charts about $x_0,y,x_2$. On the cores the maps are uniformly close to $u_{T_n}$, while on those three regions they are close because both approach the same generator. Consequently the inverse local addition between them is defined everywhere and preserves the boundary tangent domain. On each of these three chart regions write the coordinate difference $z_n=q(v_n)-q(u_{T_n})$. Choose a real cutoff equal to one outside fixed-width collars of its endpoints, vanishing smoothly before it reaches the component cores, and extend $\zeta_n=\chi_n z_n$ by zero to the whole strip. The derivatives of these cutoffs through every fixed order are bounded independently of $n$. Each $\zeta_n$ belongs to $H^3\cap\mathcal X^1$: for finite necks this follows from smoothness and finite length, and on outer tails from the actual exponential asymptotics of both finite-energy maps. There is the exact equation $$D_0\zeta_n=\chi_n' z_n-\chi_n D_0q(u_{T_n}).$$ The first term tends to zero in $H^2$, since it is supported in finitely many fixed-width translated collars of smooth component convergence. The second is zero except at the fixed-width pregluing join, where it is $O(\epsilon_{T_n})$. Apply the actual whole-strip inverse and higher regularity in [F3] to conclude $\|\zeta_n\|_{H^3}\to0$, independently of the three region lengths. On their omitted collars and the component cores convergence already holds smoothly. The inverse local-addition formula is coordinate difference on exact generator charts and a bounded smooth composition on the cores. Patching these finitely many regions therefore proves $$\|\mathcal E_{u_{T_n}}^{-1}(v_n)\|_{H^3}\longrightarrow0.$$ This argument also proves global energy convergence from these hypotheses. [F1, F3, F5, given, construct, algebra]

Fix a smooth target metric and use the translation-invariant energy density $e(u)=\tfrac12(|u_s|^2+|u_t|^2)$. Define $A^\pm(b)=\int_{[b-2,b+2]\times[0,1]}e(u^\pm)$. These smooth nonnegative functions decay with all derivatives at both infinities and have positive maxima. By [F5] choose $0<\delta<\min(\max A^-,\max A^+)$ which is a regular value of both functions. Each level set $(A^\pm)^{-1}(\delta)$ is finite: it is compact by the end decay, and its points are isolated by nonzero derivative, so an infinite set would have an accumulation point contradicting that same derivative condition. Choose a fixed $S$ containing all these crossings and sufficiently large that $A^\pm<\delta/4$ outside $[-S,S]$. Let $b_-$ be the first crossing of $A^-$ and $b_+$ the last crossing of $A^+$. These choices only use a common regular value, finite minima and maxima. [F1, F5, construct, algebra]

The corrections also have the differentiated estimates $\|\xi_R'\|_{H^3}+\|\xi_R''\|_{H^3}\le C\epsilon_R$ in these local coordinates. Indeed write $e_R=\mathcal F_R(0)$, $N_R(\xi)=\mathcal F_R(\xi)-e_R-D_R\xi$, and $\xi_R=Q_R y_R$. The fixed-point equation of [F4] is $y_R=-e_R-N_R(Q_Ry_R)$. The exact error in [F1] and its first two $R$ derivatives are $O(\epsilon_R)$ in $H^2$. The explicit local section formulas give, uniformly on a fixed small ball, $\|N_R(\xi)\|+\|\partial_R N_R(\xi)\|+\|\partial_R^2N_R(\xi)\|\le C\|\xi\|^2$, $\|d_\xi N_R(\xi)\|+\|\partial_Rd_\xi N_R(\xi)\|\le C\|\xi\|$, and bounded second $\xi$ derivative. To justify the parameter estimates, subtract the value and the linear term at zero before differentiating the coefficient formulas; each remaining Taylor term has at least two variation factors. Their $H^2$ products are bounded by the actual Sobolev algebra in [F3]. Now $\|y_R\|_{H^2}=O(\epsilon_R)$ follows from its equation and [F1]. Differentiating once gives $(I+d_\xi N_R Q_R)y_R'=-e_R'-\partial_RN_R-d_\xi N_R Q_R'y_R$. Its inverse has norm at most two for large $R$, and the right side is $O(\epsilon_R)$. Differentiate again; its highest unknown is the same invertible factor times $y_R''$, all other terms being $e_R''$, quadratic terms in $y_R,y_R'$ and bounded $Q_R',Q_R''$. They are $O(\epsilon_R)$. The product rule for $Q_Ry_R$ proves the claim. All differentiations are legitimate by the actual smooth parameter conclusion of [F4]. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

The actual zero set has uniform phase charts near $g_R$. Its derivative has a uniformly bounded right inverse by [F1], and its nonlinear derivative is uniformly Lipschitz. Use the pregluing chart centered by translation at $\xi_R$, namely $z\mapsto\mathcal E(u_R,\xi_R+z)$, so all coefficient bounds remain those of [F1]. In these centered coordinates let $P_R=I-\widetilde Q_R\widetilde D_R$. Its norm is bounded uniformly, since those of $\widetilde Q_R,\widetilde D_R$ are. The proof of [F4] gives a zero chart $k\mapsto k+h_R(k)$ over a fixed-radius ball of the kernel, with $h_R(0)=dh_R(0)=0$ and uniform first two derivative bounds after making that radius uniformly smaller. Indeed its defining contraction has ratio at most $1/2$, and its first two derivative formulas involve only the uniform right-inverse and coefficient bounds. The phase map $k\mapsto\ell_R(k+h_R(k))$ has uniformly invertible derivative at zero by step 1.3 and uniformly bounded second derivative. The explicit finite-dimensional Newton proof, shrinking the radius until the derivative differs by at most half the lower bound, gives an injective phase chart whose image contains a fixed Euclidean ball. Every zero sufficiently close in $H^3$ belongs to this chart, because its $P_R$ and $I-P_R$ components lie in the fixed product neighborhood of the contraction. Both this closeness radius and the phase ball radius can be chosen independent of $R$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.3, construct, algebra]

The family $g_R$ has a uniform bound for its longitudinal derivative in geometric $H^3$. Its uniform $H^3$ correction and [F3] give a global uniform $C^1$ bound. The local bootstrap in [F3], using finitely many target charts and fixed-radius source patches, then gives uniform bounds of every fixed derivative order. On the two fixed-width translated component cores these imply uniform Sobolev bounds. Outside those cores choose the cores large enough that $u_R$ lies in the corresponding exact generator charts; the small $C^1$ correction puts $g_R$ there as well. There its coordinate map $v$ satisfies $D_0v=0$. Cut $v$ off to zero in fixed-width collars inside those cores, separately for the two tails and middle neck. Each resulting section belongs to the whole-strip $H^1$ domain: this follows from exponential end decay on infinite tails and finiteness of each middle interval. Its $D_0$ image is supported in the finitely many collars, and has uniformly bounded $H^3$ norm by the local bootstrap. The actual inverse of $D_0$, together with the higher estimate of [F3], bounds its $H^4$ norm uniformly, independently of neck length. The omitted collars are already uniformly bounded. Thus $\|(g_R)_s\|_{H^3}\le C$. Also $\|\partial_Rg_R\|_{H^3}\le C$ by step 2.1 and the fixed-component pregluing formulas. It follows by the Banach-valued fundamental theorem that, in the uniformly valid local-addition identifications, $\|\tau_a g_{R+\rho}-g_R\|_{H^3}\le C(|a|+|\rho|)$ for uniformly small $a,\rho$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

For every sufficiently large $R$, the energy-window profile $A_R(b)=\int_{[b-2,b+2]\times[0,1]}e(g_R)$ has its first $\delta$ crossing near $-R+b_-$ and its last near $R+b_+$. To verify this globally, on each shifted compact core the profile and its first $b$ derivative converge to the respective $A^\pm$, while outside those cores it is below $\delta/2$. The latter follows from component tail smallness, the fixed join estimate and the global $H^3$ correction: $H^3\subset C^1$ bounds the change in each fixed-length window energy uniformly by $C\|\xi_R\|_{H^3}$. The derivative of a window integral is the difference of its two endpoint slice integrals, giving the same uniform bound for its $b$ derivative. Compactness of the component core complements of small crossing neighborhoods excludes any extra crossings. Nonzero derivative at each component crossing gives exactly one nearby crossing by the one-dimensional inverse theorem. Call the first and last crossings $B_L(R),B_R(R)$. They are smooth by step 1.2 and the implicit-function proof of [F4]. On the fixed translated cores step 2.1 also bounds the correction's $R$ derivative in $C^1$. The derivative identities for the pregluing there are exactly $\partial_R A_R=\partial_b A_R$ on the left and $\partial_R A_R=-\partial_b A_R$ on the right, up to $O(\epsilon_R)$ correction terms. Implicit differentiation at the crossings therefore gives $$B_L'(R)=-1+O(\epsilon_R),\qquad B_R'(R)=1+O(\epsilon_R).$$ In particular their separation $T(R)=B_R(R)-B_L(R)$ has $T'(R)>1$ after increasing $R_0$. [F1, F4, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 1.5, construct, algebra]

For $H_R(a,\rho)=\tau_a g_{R+\rho}$, evaluate the difference from $g_R$ with these same two phase tests, using the centered coordinate $\mathcal E_{u_R}^{-1}(H_R(a,\rho))-\xi_R$. At $(a,\rho)=(0,0)$ the phase derivative matrix is $$\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}+O(\epsilon_R).$$ On the left core the pregluing is $u^-(s+R,t)$, so both a longitudinal translation and increasing $R$ differentiate to $u_s^-$; on the right core increasing $R$ differentiates to $-u_s^+$ while translation differentiates to $u_s^+$. At any parameter $a$, finite linear combinations of parameter tangent directions are $C^k$ dense in the smooth compactly supported fields $Y$ on $O$ satisfying $YJ(a)+J(a)Y=0$, for every finite $k$. proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: Construct a countable collection $B_n$ of smooth endomorphism fields compactly supported in $O$, anti-commuting with $J^*$, whose finite span is dense in every finite $C^k$ norm on smooth compactly supported such fields. These are countably many fields and anti-commute with $J^*$. To verify density, split any given compactly supported field by a finite smooth partition subordinate to such relatively compact charts; an ordinary finite partition follows by finitely many bumps positive on its compact support and dividing their sum. Its local coefficient functions extend smoothly by zero. Convolution with the normalized bump at rational radii tending to zero converges with every prescribed finite number of derivatives, because differentiation commutes with convolution and the derivatives are uniformly continuous on a compact support. Choose $r>0$ so $\|B(a)\|_{C^0}<1/2$ for $\|a\|<r$, and define $$J(a)=J^*(I+B(a))(I-B(a))^{-1}.$$ The inverse is its uniformly convergent geometric series. Anti-commutation gives $(I-B)J^*=J^*(I+B)$, hence direct multiplication shows $J(a)^2=-I$. It equals $J^*$ on $P$. Matrix inversion is smooth in each $C^k$ coefficient algebra: products obey the finite Leibniz estimate, the inverse has bounded derivatives by differentiating $(I-B)R=I$, and locally its inverse is the convergent Neumann series around any invertible coefficient field. The difference identity for two inverses gives derivative $R\,dB\,R$, with a quadratic remainder, and repeated differentiation proves all higher norm derivatives. Combining with step 2.1 proves the stated compatible smooth maps $H\to C^k$. For tameness, on the compact spatial projection of $\overline O$ the continuous positive function $\omega_x(v,J_t^*v)$ on unit tangent vectors has a positive minimum $\kappa$.
